deciding_marker_or_seam: חזון with regnal frame
boundary_rationale: Keep 1:1 as the book’s vision superscription because its regnal frame is complete before the direct summons begins at 1:2. The rejected 1:1-20 unit preserves context but loses a marked genre transition; the canonical objection survives only as a non-naked-presentation warning.
defensible_basis: The noun rendered “vision,” followed by Isaiah’s Judah-and-Jerusalem scope and four-reign frame, makes 1:1 a true superscription ending at the verse boundary. Folding it into 1:2-20 obscures the formal turn from bibliographic frame to the heaven-and-earth lawsuit, although retrieval should hydrate the heading with its parent.

source_observations.text: The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.

primary_reviews.support: The Hebrew superscription supplies subject, object, geographic scope, and regnal dating within verse 1; the address to heavens starts a different speech act in verse 2.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A heading this short can become misleading when retrieved without the lawsuit it introduces.

primary_reviews.support: Bibliographic framing closes before the opening cosmic audience is summoned, so heading and accusation perform distinguishable literary work.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The superscription governs more than the immediately following oracle and therefore is not a self-contained message.

primary_reviews.support: A naked one-verse result may be mistaken for a substantive oracle instead of metadata governing the collection.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The verse is still an observable canonical form boundary and can remain a child when its parent is mandatory.

challenge.claim: Independent retrieval of 1:1 can strip the superscription from the speech it frames.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Require hydration with Isa.1.1-31, or expose 1:1 as heading metadata rather than a standalone reading unit.

deciding_marker_or_seam: heaven and earth summons through remnant observation
boundary_rationale: End the first accusation at 1:9: the remnant comparison answers the desolation sequence, while 1:10 names a new audience and shifts from national ruin to rejected sacrifice. A single 1:2-20 block is possible as a macro-lawsuit but is less precise for the two distinct addresses.
defensible_basis: The command for heavens and earth to hear launches a covenant accusation whose images move from rebellious children to a wounded body and finally a nearly erased city with a surviving remnant at 1:9. Extending through 1:20 ignores the fresh “rulers of Sodom” vocative at 1:10, which restarts the indictment around worship.

source_observations.text: Hear, heavens, and listen, earth; for Yahweh has spoken: “I have nourished and brought up children and they have rebelled against me.
Unless Yahweh of Armies had left to us a very small remnant, we would have been as Sodom. We would have been like Gomorrah.

primary_reviews.support: The opening imperatives summon cosmic witnesses, and the remnant conditional at 1:9 gives the devastation catalogue a grammatical and rhetorical close.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The lawsuit accusation continues conceptually into the cultic charges that follow.

primary_reviews.support: Rebellious-family, diseased-body, and besieged-city images form a descending sequence completed by the Sodom survival comparison.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verses 2-20 together can be heard as one broad prosecution and invitation.

primary_reviews.support: No internal cross-reference independently establishes 1:9 as a retrieval seam; the decision rests on the local address and image progression.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Keeping 1:2-9 inside the full 1:1-31 parent protects the larger lawsuit setting.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Sodom address reset and mouth-of-YHWH close
boundary_rationale: Retain 1:10-20 as the worship indictment and cleansing appeal, ending where the divine-mouth attestation seals its alternatives. The broader 1:2-20 proposal has thematic continuity, yet the exact audience change at 1:10 and formal closure at 1:20 make the narrower movement more defensible.
defensible_basis: “Hear” and “listen” addressed to Sodom and Gomorrah begin a new disputation about sacrifices, assemblies, prayer, cleansing, and willing obedience. The unit closes at 1:20 with the antithetical eat/be-eaten verdict and the mouth-of-YHWH formula; absorbing 1:2-9 would erase the vocative reset and its cultic focus.

source_observations.text: Hear Yahweh’s word, you rulers of Sodom! Listen to the law of our God, you people of Gomorrah!
but if you refuse and rebel, you will be devoured with the sword; for Yahweh’s mouth has spoken it.”

primary_reviews.support: Paired hearing imperatives open the address, and the concluding ki pi YHWH dibber formula marks the stated choice as complete at verse 20.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Sodom language also echoes verse 9, binding this speech to the preceding devastation accusation.

primary_reviews.support: Rejected ritual, bloodstained hands, washing, justice, and the color reversal advance as one accusation-to-invitation arc.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The larger lawsuit begun at 1:2 remains the governing parent and should accompany isolated retrieval.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical reuse may illuminate individual lines, but it cannot choose between the local 1:10-20 child and the 1:2-20 macro-unit.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The explicit 1:10 address and 1:20 seal provide adequate local evidence without importing later usage.

deciding_marker_or_seam: איכה city lament resolves through metallurgy and fire
boundary_rationale: Keep 1:21-31 together because the lament’s city question receives its complete judicial and metallurgical answer before the unquenchable-fire ending. The proposed 1:24 seam recognizes a divine-speech turn but produces accusation and remedy fragments that depend on one another more than either gains from separate retrieval.
rejected_alternative: split 1:24-31 away from the lament it answers
defensible_basis: The exclamation “How has the faithful city become a prostitute?” opens a city lament whose corrupt silver, rulers, and injustice are answered by smelting, restored judges, and the final oak-and-garden fire at 1:31. Splitting at 1:24 detaches the announced purification from the civic corruption it directly resolves.

source_observations.text: How the faithful city has become a prostitute! She was full of justice. Righteousness lodged in her, but now there are murderers.
The strong will be like tinder, and his work like a spark. They will both burn together, and no one will quench them.”

primary_reviews.support: The opening lament particle introduces the city’s reversal, while the adversative divine declaration at 1:24 answers rather than abandons that complaint.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 24 has a messenger-style declaration and could be treated as the start of a judgment response.

primary_reviews.support: Debased metal at the accusation is reversed by smelting in the answer, and the oak/garden combustion supplies the poem’s terminal image.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The response contains its own restoration and judgment movements that could be internal children.

primary_reviews.support: Separating 1:24-31 risks presenting purification without the city conditions named in 1:21-23; the integrated child retains the problem-solution relation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A user seeking the restoration oracle may prefer a hydrated 1:24-31 child.

deciding_marker_or_seam: הדבר אשר חזה is an explicit localized heading
boundary_rationale: Surface 2:1 as a heading because its formula identifies the message and its scope, whereas 2:2 begins with an eschatological time expression and poetic scene. The literary proposal to keep 2:1-5 together remains a presentation alternative, not a reason to deny the observed heading boundary.
rejected_alternative: treat the heading as the first poetic line
defensible_basis: The phrase “the word that Isaiah son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem” is a localized prophetic heading complete at 2:1, before the latter-days poem begins. Treating it as the first poetic line confuses its framing syntax with the following vision, though the one-verse child must travel with the 2:1-22 parent in retrieval.

source_observations.text: This is what Isaiah the son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem.

primary_reviews.support: Hadavar asher hazah plus prophet and geographic object constitutes a nominal heading; the temporal vehayah be’acharit hayyamim starts at verse 2.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Masoretic presentation does not itself decide whether the heading should be a standalone retrieval result.

primary_reviews.support: Heading, nations poem, and house-of-Jacob exhortation can be read as a single 2:1-5 Zion movement before the causal turn at 2:6.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The superscription has a distinct framing function and verse 2 supplies the poem’s actual temporal opening.

challenge.claim: A separate 2:1 child may overstate the independence of a heading that introduces 2:2-5.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Offer 2:1-5 as the surfaced child while preserving 2:1 as internal heading metadata.

primary_reviews.support: Parallel prophetic wording elsewhere confirms the heading genre but does not settle whether it is returned independently.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Mandatory 2:1-22 hydration can make the local formal boundary operationally safe.

deciding_marker_or_seam: latter-days opening resolves in weapons-to-agriculture reversal
boundary_rationale: End the nations instruction poem at 2:4, where its movement from ascent to Torah to international judgment culminates in disarmament. The 2:1-5 alternative preserves an exhortational echo, but verse 5 changes audience and grammatical force and therefore does not outweigh the completed poetic tableau.
defensible_basis: The latter-days scene gathers nations to Zion for instruction and reaches its own reversal when weapons become agricultural tools and war training ceases at 2:4. Adding 2:5 changes from third-person nations imagery to a direct house-of-Jacob imperative, so the exhortation works better as the hinge into the abasement oracle.

source_observations.text: It shall happen in the latter days, that the mountain of Yahweh’s house shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it.

He will judge between the nations, and will decide concerning many peoples. They shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.

primary_reviews.support: The sequence of plural nation speech and divine adjudication closes with paired negated war clauses; verse 5 begins a second-person plural summons.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The “light of YHWH” exhortation may function as the poem’s intended application rather than the next unit’s opening.

primary_reviews.support: Verse 5 answers the nations’ “come, let us go up” language and can complete a 2:1-5 call-and-response pattern.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The international peace image already has terminal balance at 2:4, and the named audience changes in 2:5.

challenge.claim: Removing 2:5 may separate the house-of-Jacob response from the nations’ Zion pilgrimage.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Test 2:1-5 as a hydrated literary child and begin the pride indictment at the explicit causal clause in 2:6.

primary_reviews.support: A 2:2-4 result preserves the famous vision as a complete scene when the heading and neighboring exhortation are supplied by parent hydration.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Without that context, users may miss both the Isaiah heading and the address to Jacob.

deciding_marker_or_seam: house-of-Jacob imperative leads into pride catalogue and cave-terror close
boundary_rationale: Preserve 2:5-22 as the abasement oracle because verse 5 names its audience and ethical summons, while verse 22 closes with a final imperative about humanity. The rival 2:6 opening is grammatically attractive after “for,” but it makes the indictment explanatory material with no surfaced exhortational frame.
rejected_alternative: surface 2:1-5 and begin the indictment at 2:6
defensible_basis: The house-of-Jacob command to walk in divine light at 2:5 becomes the standard against which abandonment, wealth, idols, and human pride are exposed. Repeated day-of-YHWH abasement and cave-terror motifs carry the speech to the command to stop trusting mortals at 2:22; starting at 2:6 weakens the governing imperative.

source_observations.text: House of Jacob, come, and let’s walk in the light of Yahweh.
Stop trusting in man, whose breath is in his nostrils; for of what account is he?

primary_reviews.support: Verse 5 is an imperative to Jacob, but the causal ki at 2:6 can attach what follows either as grounds for that command or as a distinct accusation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Repetition of being humbled and entering rocks still unifies 2:6-22 independently of verse 5.

primary_reviews.support: The exhortation in 2:5 echoes the ascent poem and may close 2:1-5, leaving the sustained day-and-pride indictment to start at 2:6.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Using verse 5 as the oracle’s thesis gives the following catalogue a clear audience and moral contrast.

challenge.claim: The active start assigns the hinge verse forward despite its lexical echo with 2:2-4.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Compare retrieval of 2:1-5 plus 2:6-22 against the frozen 2:2-4 plus 2:5-22 route, retaining both in the dissent ledger.

primary_reviews.support: Beginning with “house of Jacob” prevents a detached judgment catalogue from appearing as an unaddressed universal abstraction.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Parent hydration already identifies the larger Zion-and-abasement cycle, so 2:6 can remain intelligible.

deciding_marker_or_seam: support-removal formula reaches the courtroom poor-ground charge
boundary_rationale: Close the leadership and courtroom movement at 3:15, after the accusation against those who grind the faces of the poor. The daughters-of-Zion speech beginning at 3:16 shares the city’s judgment setting but introduces a new addressee, imagery system, and consequence extending across the chapter boundary.
defensible_basis: The removal of every support in Jerusalem opens a leadership-collapse oracle that proceeds through social inversion and culminates in YHWH standing to judge elders and princes for crushing the poor at 3:15. Continuing into 3:16 would cross a new “daughters of Zion” subject and a different body-adornment judgment.

source_observations.text: For, behold, the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, takes away from Jerusalem and from Judah supply and support, the whole supply of bread, and the whole supply of water;
What do you mean that you crush my people, and grind the face of the poor?” says the Lord, Yahweh of Armies.

primary_reviews.support: Removal formulae and leadership nouns dominate 3:1-12; the courtroom stance and direct elder-prince accusation complete that concern in 3:13-15.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The messenger declaration in 3:16 remains within the same broad Jerusalem judgment discourse.

primary_reviews.support: The unit moves coherently from institutional deprivation to chaotic replacements and then to judicial accountability for failed governance.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A chapter-scale 3:1-4:1 composition would keep all social groups inside one collapse tableau.

primary_reviews.support: Retrieving through 3:15 preserves the causal link between leadership failure and harm to vulnerable people instead of isolating the courtroom charge.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The subsequent address supplies another concrete manifestation of the city’s pride and loss.

deciding_marker_or_seam: fresh daughters-of-Zion vocative continues through the seven-women close
boundary_rationale: Use the cross-chapter 3:16-4:1 span because its female addressee, adornment reversal, male-loss lament, and seven-women outcome form one descending sequence. The 3:26 endpoint follows a printed division rather than the action, while 4:2 unmistakably resets with a restoration formula.
defensible_basis: A fresh declaration about the daughters of Zion begins at 3:16, catalogues ornament and its removal, reaches city desolation at 3:26, and continues naturally to seven women seeking one man in 4:1. Stopping at the chapter number would sever that final social consequence from the population-loss judgment that produces it.

source_observations.text: Moreover Yahweh said, “Because the daughters of Zion are arrogant, and walk with outstretched necks and flirting eyes, walking daintily as they go, jingling ornaments on their feet;
Seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying, “We will eat our own bread, and wear our own clothing. Just let us be called by your name. Take away our reproach.”

primary_reviews.support: The opening wayyo’mer plus daughters-of-Zion subject governs the punishment catalogue; 4:1 continues with feminine action before 4:2’s “in that day” renewal.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 3:26 has a strong city-lament image that can sound like a poetic close.

primary_reviews.support: Adornment becomes shame, men fall, gates lament, and the scarcity scene in 4:1 supplies the social aftermath rather than a new episode.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The shift from plural daughters to seven women could be treated as a brief concluding child.

primary_reviews.support: Crossing the chapter protects the causal sequence and exposes a mechanical chapter split as the weaker retrieval boundary.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The unit still needs the larger 3:1-4:6 parent to avoid detaching it from leadership judgment and later restoration.

deciding_marker_or_seam: in-that-day branch reset reaches the canopy refuge close
boundary_rationale: Retain 4:2-6 as the purified-Zion restoration oracle because its remnant and cleansing movement resolves in a complete protective-canopy image. Both neighboring alternatives lose to marked form changes: 4:1 concludes scarcity, and 5:1 begins a first-person song for the beloved.
defensible_basis: “In that day” at 4:2 reverses the preceding shame with branch, surviving remnant, cleansing, renewed cloud-and-fire, canopy, shade, and refuge, ending at 4:6. Attaching 4:1 would import the prior judgment’s final consequence; continuing into 5:1 would cross into an explicitly introduced vineyard song.

source_observations.text: In that day, Yahweh’s branch will be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land will be the beauty and glory of the survivors of Israel.
There will be a pavilion for a shade in the daytime from the heat, and for a refuge and for a shelter from storm and from rain.

primary_reviews.support: Bayyom hahu opens the reversal, and creation/cloud/tabernacle language develops without a new speech formula through the refuge close.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The same temporal formula recurs frequently and cannot establish a seam by itself.

primary_reviews.support: Purification of survivors leads to protective presence over the assembly, giving the short restoration poem an internal beginning, transformation, and sheltering result.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its meaning is intentionally contrastive with 3:16-4:1 and should retain parent-level linkage.

primary_reviews.support: A separate child allows the restoration movement to be found without swallowing the preceding judgment, while parent hydration keeps their designed contrast visible.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Isolated retrieval may invite identity claims about the “branch” that local chunking cannot decide.

deciding_marker_or_seam: song invitation is completed by explicit vineyard identification
boundary_rationale: Keep 5:1-7 intact as vineyard song plus juridical interpretation, ending where the expected justice/righteousness contrasts are decoded. An independent 5:1-6 poem is formally possible, but its withheld referents and courtroom question make verse 7 the necessary completion rather than an optional appendix.
defensible_basis: The invitation to sing for the beloved introduces vineyard preparation, failed fruit, a judicial appeal, and threatened dismantling; 5:7 then identifies vineyard, plants, justice, and bloodshed in matching wordplay. Splitting before the interpretation leaves the song’s legal riddle unanswered, while 5:8 begins a new woe catalogue.

source_observations.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill.
For the vineyard of Yahweh of Armies is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant. He looked for justice, but behold, oppression, for righteousness, but behold, a cry of distress.

primary_reviews.support: The first-person song shifts to direct vineyard address and then to the explanatory ki; the justice/bloodshed and righteousness/cry paronomasia seals the interpretation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 7 changes from figurative narrative to explicit prophetic application and can be marked internally.

primary_reviews.support: Love song, disappointed cultivation, audience verdict, destruction sentence, and riddle solution constitute one carefully staged forensic performance.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A reader studying poetic form may want the song proper distinguished from its interpretive gloss.

primary_reviews.support: Returning the metaphor without verse 7 would encourage uncontrolled identification; including the interpretation anchors the vineyard’s local function.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later vineyard reuse can illuminate reception but must not determine this seam.

deciding_marker_or_seam: repeated הוי accusations resolve in causal root-and-blossom judgment
boundary_rationale: Treat 5:8-24 as the woe catalogue because recurring accusation-and-verdict panels accumulate toward the rejected-instruction summary at its endpoint. Six smaller sayings remain useful internal movements, but none gains enough independence to outweigh the catalogue’s shared forensic function and final causal judgment.
defensible_basis: A chain of repeated “woe” accusations addresses land accumulation, drunken feasting, deliberate sin, moral inversion, self-wisdom, and corrupt justice, with matching consequences. The root-and-blossom fire image closes this governed catalogue at 5:24; atomizing each woe loses their cumulative prosecution, whereas 5:25 changes to the anger refrain and invasion horizon.

source_observations.text: Woe to those who join house to house, who lay field to field, until there is no room, and you are made to dwell alone in the middle of the land!

Therefore as the tongue of fire devours the stubble, and as the dry grass sinks down in the flame, so their root shall be as rottenness, and their blossom shall go up as dust, because they have rejected the law of Yahweh of Armies, and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel.

primary_reviews.support: Repeated hoy openings mark coordinated strophes, and the final al-ken clause explains their destruction by rejection of divine instruction.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Each woe has a distinct addressee, image, and sanction and could be separately retrieved with siblings.

primary_reviews.support: The catalogue escalates from property and appetite to speech, moral categories, wisdom claims, and public justice before a consuming verdict.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A six-child representation would expose the patterned architecture more explicitly.

primary_reviews.support: The larger unit prevents one accusation from being detached from parallel charges and their common legal conclusion.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Search precision for a particular woe may require internal anchors without promoting them to top-level chunks.

deciding_marker_or_seam: anger and outstretched-hand turn introduces signal and invasion tableau
boundary_rationale: Place 5:25 forward with 5:26-30 because the anger refrain opens a new scale of judgment and the signal-to-nations sequence completes it at the darkness ending. The backward attachment to the sixth woe remains plausible grammatical dissent, but the frozen boundary better preserves the invasion tableau as a whole.
rejected_alternative: attach 5:25 to the final woe and end at 5:24
defensible_basis: The therefore clause at 5:25 introduces divine anger, earthquake, corpses, and the first outstretched-hand refrain, then 5:26-30 expands the threat into a summoned distant army ending in sea-like darkness. Attaching verse 25 backward respects causation but leaves its refrain and invasion imagery separated from the coda they initiate.

source_observations.text: Therefore Yahweh’s anger burns against his people, and he has stretched out his hand against them and has struck them. The mountains tremble, and their dead bodies are as refuse in the middle of the streets. For all this, his anger is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.
They will roar against them in that day like the roaring of the sea. If one looks to the land, behold, darkness and distress. The light is darkened in its clouds.

primary_reviews.support: The al-ken at 5:25 points backward to rejected instruction in 5:24, and the anger refrain can function as the preceding woe catalogue’s sentence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The same verse introduces the recurring outstretched-hand formula and landscape of national attack developed through verse 30.

challenge.claim: The causal particle and judgment refrain make 5:25 a credible close for 5:8-25.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Preserve a competing 5:8-25 plus 5:26-30 route for later Hebrew discourse adjudication.

primary_reviews.support: Earthquake devastation broadens into the banner, swift invaders, roaring, and darkened land, producing one cinematic coda after the local woes.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 25 has retrospective logic and could serve as a hinge shared by both movements.

primary_reviews.support: Retrieval beginning at 5:25 may hide the therefore relation to the catalogue’s final rejection-of-instruction verdict.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Hydrating 5:25-30 with the full chapter retains that cause while keeping the invasion sequence undivided.

challenge.claim: The frozen child starts with a backward-pointing conclusion that may appear causeless.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Require chapter-parent hydration and retain 5:25-backward attachment as an append-only boundary appeal.

deciding_marker_or_seam: dated throne scene contains completed purification commission and stump coda
boundary_rationale: Preserve all of chapter 6 as the dated throne-vision commission: every stage advances one scene, and the stump coda answers the prophet’s duration question. Smaller vision, purification, and commissioning movements are real internal parts, but the continuous speaker exchange gives no better surfaced endpoint before 6:13.
defensible_basis: The death-year date opens a throne vision whose holiness acclamation, smoke, confession, coal purification, commission dialogue, hardening instruction, how-long question, devastation, and stump image run through 6:13. Splits at 6:8 or 6:9 sever preparation from the commission it enables or command from its requested duration.

source_observations.text: In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple.
If there is a tenth left in it, that also will in turn be consumed, as a terebinth, and as an oak whose stump remains when they are cut down, so the holy seed is its stump.”

primary_reviews.support: Narrative wayyiqtol sequencing, direct speech, and the prophet’s reply remain continuous from the throne sight through the final seed metaphor.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The whom-shall-I-send question at 6:8 and imperative at 6:9 are strong internal discourse turns.

primary_reviews.support: Vision, unworthiness, cleansing, volunteering, commission, protest, and answer form a single call narrative with no unresolved action.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Independent retrieval of 6:1-8 or 6:9-13 could serve form-specific study if compulsory siblings accompany it.

primary_reviews.support: Keeping the scene whole guards against quoting either the holiness acclamation or hardening commission without the narrative response around it.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A whole-chapter unit may receive a mechanical confidence penalty despite strong literary evidence.

deciding_marker_or_seam: dated encounter named child and faith warning complete the first exchange
boundary_rationale: End the initial crisis encounter at the faith warning in 7:9 because its narrative setup and first oracle are complete before YHWH spoke again reopens the exchange. The 7:1-17 parent is valuable for hydration, but it masks two distinct speech rounds and their different rhetorical functions.
defensible_basis: A dated coalition crisis brings Ahaz, Isaiah, and the named child to the aqueduct, followed by the command not to fear, the enemies’ plan, and the faith warning at 7:9. Extending through 7:17 merges this first reassurance with a renewed divine speech and Ahaz’s separate refusal-and-sign dialogue beginning in 7:10.

source_observations.text: In the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah, Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to war against it, but could not prevail against it.
The head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is Remaliah’s son. If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established.’”

primary_reviews.support: Dating and movement to the conduit establish the scene; the paired im-lo ta’aminu and lo te’amenu wordplay gives the first speech a terminal warning.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The same encounter and addressee continue after verse 9, so the seam is a speech-round boundary rather than a scene change.

primary_reviews.support: Fear report, symbolic child, reassurance, adversary plan, counter-oracle, and faith condition complete the first dramatic exchange.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A single 7:1-17 child would keep the reassurance and sign controversy together.

primary_reviews.support: Separate retrieval reduces the tendency to isolate the later sign verse while the 7:1-17 parent preserves the common political scene.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Users can misread 7:9 as the final outcome unless the renewed speech at 7:10 is visible.

deciding_marker_or_seam: YHWH-spoke-again reset reaches the sign and child-time horizon
boundary_rationale: Keep 7:10-17 as the royal sign dialogue and oracle, closing when the promised time scale reaches the announced political reversal. The famous central verse is not its own literary unit, and the repeated temporal panels after verse 17 are a new sequence despite thematic continuity.
defensible_basis: The renewed speech formula at 7:10 initiates an offer, Ahaz’s refusal, prophetic rebuke, sign announcement, and child-time horizon concluding with the king-of-Assyria threat at 7:17. Isolating 7:14 strips the sign from its dialogue; carrying 7:18-25 forward would absorb four new in-that-day devastation panels.

source_observations.text: Yahweh spoke again to Ahaz, saying,
Yahweh will bring on you, on your people, and on your father’s house days that have not come, from the day that Ephraim departed from Judah, even the king of Assyria.

primary_reviews.support: The dialogue boundaries are clear, but lexical and translation disputes within the sign wording cannot be settled from the correlated OSHB and UXLC witnesses alone.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Those unresolved semantic questions do not erase the renewed-speech opening or the 7:17 endpoint.

primary_reviews.support: Offer, refusal, rebuke, sign, naming, diet, discernment horizon, and land consequence unfold as one tightly linked exchange.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The threat at 7:17 also introduces Assyria, the agent governing the next devastation cycle.

primary_reviews.support: The full dialogue prevents a celebrated sign line from being detached from speaker, audience, refusal, and temporal framing.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later canonical reuse is important context but neither identifies the child nor authorizes a preferred translation here.

deciding_marker_or_seam: four repeated in-that-day panels govern the devastation sequence
boundary_rationale: Surface 7:18-25 as the land-devastation cycle because its four temporal panels share Assyrian aftermath imagery and reach a complete agricultural desolation close. The following writing-and-naming episode has a distinct action frame, so mere continuity of crisis does not justify combining them.
rejected_alternative: merge the new chapter-8 sign action
defensible_basis: Four repeated in-that-day openings organize fly-and-bee summoning, humiliating shaving, subsistence food, and briar-covered land, ending with fear of thorns at 7:25. Merging chapter 8 would cross from this panoramic sequence into a commanded tablet, named witnesses, conception, and a new symbolic sign action.

source_observations.text: It will happen in that day that Yahweh will whistle for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria.

deciding_marker_or_seam: sustained Moab lament and appeal reaches explicit former-now timed close
boundary_rationale: Retain 15:1-16:14 as the Moab lament burden with timed epilogue because target, grief register, flight, appeal, pride, failed worship, and deadline remain one governed dossier. The 15:1-16:5, 16:6-12, and 16:13-14 divisions are defensible internal forms, preserved as dissent but not promoted here.
rejected_alternative: surface three literary children as independent units
defensible_basis: The Moab burden sustains ruined-city cries, ascent and shaving lament, flight, waters, refugees, tribute appeal, proposed throne shelter, pride accusation, vineyard grief, failed sanctuary prayer, and an explicit former-word-now-three-years epilogue ending at 16:14. Surfacing three children clarifies movements but risks detaching the timed update from the burden it revises.

source_observations.text: The burden of Moab. For in a night, Ar of Moab is laid waste, and brought to nothing. For in a night Kir of Moab is laid waste, and brought to nothing.

But now Yahweh has spoken, saying, “Within three years, as a worker bound by contract would count them, the glory of Moab shall be brought into contempt, with all his great multitude; and the remnant will be very small and feeble.”

primary_reviews.support: The Moab burden heading governs repeated place names and lament verbs; zeh haddavar and ve’atta dibber at 16:13-14 explicitly label the deadline as a later speech about that same oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The former-word/now contrast makes 16:13-14 a distinct editorial or prophetic postscript with strong independent form.

primary_reviews.support: Lament-and-appeal through 16:5, pride-and-vineyard grief in 16:6-12, and the timed epilogue at 16:13-14 each possess recognizable local contours.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The latter movements answer the refugee appeal and remain explicitly about Moab under one burden heading.

challenge.claim: The active parent may be too coarse for three internally complete rhetorical movements.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Test three hydrated children while preserving 15:1-16:14 as their mandatory oracle parent.

primary_reviews.support: The larger span prevents the throne appeal, pride indictment, or three-year deadline from appearing without the Moab lament that gives each function.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A two-chapter result is costly for focused retrieval unless internal anchors and parent-sibling navigation are available.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Damascus burden reaches failed-planting verdict
boundary_rationale: Close the Damascus-Ephraim burden at 17:11 because its city, glory, remnant, altar, and planting motifs reach a direct harvest-loss verdict there. The nations woe after it shares threat language but introduces its own exclamation, soundscape, rebuke, and evening-to-morning temporal miniature.
defensible_basis: The Damascus burden opens with ruined-city and diminished-Jacob judgments, turns through gleaning and in-that-day regard for the Maker, contrasts abandoned strong cities, and ends with failed pleasant plantings and incurable grief at 17:11. Adding 17:12-14 would cross a fresh woe cry and a new roaring-nations image.

source_observations.text: The burden of Damascus. “Behold, Damascus is taken away from being a city, and it will be a ruinous heap.
In the day of your planting, you hedge it in. In the morning, you make your seed blossom, but the harvest flees away in the day of grief and of desperate sorrow.

primary_reviews.support: Massa Dammeseq sets the target; gleaning, Maker-altars contrast, and the harvest-day result proceed without a new heading through verse 11.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verses 12-14 may broaden the same adversarial horizon from named cities to unnamed peoples.

primary_reviews.support: Loss moves from city to glory to harvest to cultic memory to doomed garden, providing a completed chain of diminishment.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The in-that-day panels at 17:4 and 17:7 are strong internal turns that could be indexed below the parent.

primary_reviews.support: Ending at failed harvest keeps the named burden distinct from the generic nations woe and avoids target confusion in retrieval.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The Damascus and Jacob association remains interpretive context, not permission to harmonize historical sequences.

deciding_marker_or_seam: fresh הוי roaring nations turns from evening terror to morning absence
boundary_rationale: Surface 17:12-14 as the roaring-nations coda because the woe cry, water similes, rebuke, flight, and overnight disappearance create a compact closed oracle. Its relation to chapter 18 or earlier invasion themes may inform context, but neither supplies a stronger boundary than the 17:12 opening and 17:14 morning close.
defensible_basis: A new woe at 17:12 compares tumultuous peoples to seas and mighty waters, then divine rebuke sends them like chaff and tumbleweed; evening terror becomes morning absence at 17:14. Retaining the whole chapter would bury this self-contained sound-and-time reversal beneath the preceding Damascus burden.

source_observations.text: Ah, the uproar of many peoples who roar like the roaring of the seas; and the rushing of nations that rush like the rushing of mighty waters!
At evening, behold, terror! Before the morning, they are no more. This is the portion of those who plunder us, and the lot of those who rob us.

primary_reviews.support: Hoy opens plural tumult, repeated hamon/sha’on sound words build intensity, and the evening/morning antithesis gives the unit a crisp closure.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The final “portion of those who plunder us” can sound like a generalized coda to preceding national judgments.

primary_reviews.support: Roar, rebuke, dispersal, dusk fear, and dawn absence form a complete miniature dominated by auditory and temporal reversal.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its brevity and generic target make it dependent on surrounding nation-oracle context.

primary_reviews.support: The narrow child is justified by form rather than fame, provided the 17:1-18:7 neighborhood remains available for orientation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Canonical analogies to sea-tumult should not be allowed to name the nations or move the seam.

deciding_marker_or_seam: distant-land vocative envoy and harvest sequence reaches tribute close
boundary_rationale: Keep 18:1-7 as the Cush envoy-harvest oracle because distant mission, universal signal, quiet divine observation, pre-harvest cutting, abandoned carcasses, and tribute arrive in one arc. No internal change supplies an endpoint comparable to the chapter’s final return to the named people and place.
defensible_basis: The woe to the land of winged boats opens with envoys and a call for all inhabitants to watch the raised banner, pauses for a divine harvest observation, then depicts pruning before ripeness and ends with tribute brought to Zion at 18:7. Dividing envoy and harvest sections would separate summons, observed action, and outcome.

source_observations.text: Ah, the land of the rustling of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia;

In that time, a present will be brought to Yahweh of Armies from a people tall and smooth, even from a people awesome from their beginning onward, a nation that measures out and treads down, whose land the rivers divide, to the place of the name of Yahweh of Armies, Mount Zion.

primary_reviews.support: Hoy identifies the distant land; imperative messenger speech yields to ki koh amar YHWH, and ba’et hahi returns to the described people for the closing gift.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The messenger commission and divine harvest saying have different speakers and could be marked as component speeches.

primary_reviews.support: Dispatch, global visibility, waiting, ripening, pruning, exposure, and eventual tribute turn diplomatic imagery into a complete prophetic tableau.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The exact relation between the envoys and harvest remains implicit, which weakens fine-grained causal claims.

primary_reviews.support: Whole-chapter retrieval keeps the difficult images together and discourages assigning the distant people a settled identity from isolated lines.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The unit’s chapter coincidence requires confidence calibration under T467 even though the literary boundaries are strong.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Egypt burden reaches failed-counsel and no-work close
boundary_rationale: Retain 19:1-15 as the Egypt judgment and failed-counsel oracle because environmental, economic, religious, and political disintegration converge on the no-work verdict. The six future-day panels that follow reverse the rhetorical direction and therefore belong to a second movement under the same chapter parent.
defensible_basis: The Egypt burden begins with divine arrival, civic conflict, emptied spirit, failed counsel, harsh rule, Nile collapse, ruined industries, foolish princes, and staggering leadership, ending at 19:15 with no work for head or tail. Extending into 19:16 would cross the first of coordinated in-that-day transformation panels.

source_observations.text: The burden of Egypt. “Behold, Yahweh rides on a swift cloud, and comes to Egypt. The idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence; and the heart of Egypt will melt within it.
Neither shall there be any work for Egypt, which head or tail, palm branch or rush, may do.

primary_reviews.support: Massa Mitsrayim opens the burden; counsel and wisdom vocabulary dominates its center, and the head-tail/palm-reed merism closes the collapse comprehensively.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The chapter’s later transformation presupposes this judgment and could be retained in one judgment-to-blessing parent.

primary_reviews.support: Divine arrival cascades through society, river economy, crafts, court wisdom, and national agency until every status level is immobilized.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The environmental and failed-counsel sections are internally distinct enough for subordinate anchors.

primary_reviews.support: Separating at verse 15 prevents the judgment catalogue from swallowing the surprising worship-and-blessing reversals that deserve their own governed child.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Both units need the 19:1-25 parent so judgment and transformation are not presented as contradictory isolated predictions.

deciding_marker_or_seam: coordinated in-that-day panels culminate in triadic blessing
boundary_rationale: Keep 19:16-25 as the in-that-day transformation cycle because repeated temporal openings stage successive changes whose climax blesses Egypt, Assyria, and Israel together. The panels are individually indexable, but their ordered expansion—not any one refrain alone—provides the unit’s completed rhetorical action.
defensible_basis: Six coordinated in-that-day panels move Egypt from trembling fear to Judah-awareness, five oath-speaking cities, an altar and pillar, cry-and-deliverance, reciprocal knowing and healing, a highway with Assyria, and finally a three-nation blessing at 19:25. Atomizing each formula would hide the cumulative transformation from terror to shared blessing.

source_observations.text: In that day the Egyptians will be like women. They will tremble and fear because of the shaking of Yahweh of Armies’s hand, which he shakes over them.
because Yahweh of Armies has blessed them, saying, “Blessed be Egypt my people, Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance.”

primary_reviews.support: Bayyom hahu marks the panels at verses 16, 18, 19, 23, and 24, while blessing language at verse 25 supplies the cycle’s final divine speech.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Formula repetition also creates several clean internal seams rather than proving only a single large unit.

primary_reviews.support: Fear becomes speech, worship, answered distress, mutual knowledge, healed relations, open travel, and a triadic blessing in deliberate escalation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The altar-pillar and highway panels have enough independent imagery to be hydrated children.

primary_reviews.support: The complete sequence reduces the risk of extracting one nation or blessing line from the chapter’s progressive reconciliation movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No boundary claim may use later canonical theology to decide the identities or status of the three named peoples.

deciding_marker_or_seam: dated commander arrival sign command and coastland interpretation complete the scene
boundary_rationale: Retain 20:1-6 as the dated prophetic sign-action narrative because its opening synchronism, command, execution, duration, interpretation, and concluding coastland question complete one scene. The prior Egypt oracle and following wilderness-sea burden differ in form even where their geopolitical vocabulary overlaps.
defensible_basis: The commander’s arrival at Ashdod dates a prose sign scene in which YHWH orders Isaiah to remove sackcloth and sandals, the prophet complies, and the three-year action is interpreted concerning Egypt and Cush before coastland observers voice dismay at 20:6. Merging adjacent poetry would blur date, enacted sign, explanation, and audience response.

source_observations.text: In the year that Tartan came to Ashdod, when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him, and he fought against Ashdod and took it;
The inhabitants of this coast land will say in that day, ‘Behold, this is our expectation, where we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria. And we, how will we escape?’”

primary_reviews.support: A historical time clause opens narrative sequencing; commanded halok and performed ken asah are answered by the ka’asher interpretation before the audience’s concluding speech.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The sign’s referents and political setting connect tightly to the surrounding nation-oracle collection.

primary_reviews.support: Date, commission, bodily performance, symbolic duration, named interpretation, and witness reaction follow the standard shape of a complete sign report.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 1’s imperial event may be introductory context rather than part of the performed action proper.

primary_reviews.support: Keeping the explanation and coastland response with the action prevents the prophet’s conduct from being retrieved as an unexplained anecdote.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Historical cross-references may inform context but cannot settle chronology or source dependence within this candidate task.

deciding_marker_or_seam: burden heading reaches fallen-Babylon report and threshing address
boundary_rationale: Keep 21:1-10 as the wilderness-sea vision and watchman report because burden, bodily response, surveillance, reported sight, fall announcement, and threshing address answer one another. A 1-5/6-10 division identifies a genuine scene turn, but neither half is as complete independently as the combined vision-report form.
defensible_basis: The wilderness-of-the-sea burden opens a harsh vision, records anguish and disrupted banquet, then receives a watchman command at 21:6 whose report of riders culminates in “Babylon is fallen” and an address to the threshed people at 21:10. Splitting at verse 6 separates the distressing vision from the commissioned observation that interprets it.

source_observations.text: The burden of the wilderness of the sea. As whirlwinds in the South sweep through, it comes from the wilderness, from an awesome land.
You are my threshing, and the grain of my floor!” That which I have heard from Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, I have declared to you.

primary_reviews.support: Massa opens the vision; ki koh amar at verse 6 commissions the lookout, whose shouted report and heard-from-YHWH attestation close the oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The command to station a watchman supplies a strong new speech and action boundary within the burden.

primary_reviews.support: Approaching storm, seer anguish, interrupted feast, patient lookout, rider report, city fall, and audience interpretation make one suspense-and-disclosure sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verses 1-5 and 6-10 could function as vision and interpretation children under mandatory parent hydration.

primary_reviews.support: The explicit watchman commission at 21:6 creates a retrievable report with its own task, observation, and announcement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Without 21:1-5, the report loses the burden heading and embodied prophetic reaction that frames its urgency.

challenge.claim: The frozen parent may be too broad for a complete 21:6-10 watchman-report child.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Retain 21:1-5 and 21:6-10 as a hydrated-child alternative without changing the current parent route.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Dumah burden and repeated watchman query form compact dialogue
boundary_rationale: Surface 21:11-12 as the Dumah watchman dialogue: address, doubled nocturnal question, paradoxical response, and invitation form a complete two-verse exchange. Its brevity is structurally warranted by the new Arabia burden at 21:13, not by a desire to isolate a famous saying.
defensible_basis: The Dumah burden consists of a repeated question from Seir—watchman, what of the night?—and the watchman’s dawn-yet-night answer with an invitation to inquire and return, ending at 21:12. Merging the Arabia burden would cross to a new heading, geographic setting, and refugee-supply action.

source_observations.text: The burden of Dumah. One calls to me out of Seir, “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?”
The watchman said, “The morning comes, and also the night. If you will inquire, inquire. Come back again.”

primary_reviews.support: Massa Dumah identifies the unit, and direct qore elay plus repeated mah-millaylah lead to the watchman’s bounded answer and return imperative.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The enigmatic answer lacks narrative resolution and remains dependent on the nation-oracle setting.

primary_reviews.support: Caller, repeated question, dawn/night paradox, and invitation to return constitute an intentionally compressed oracle-dialogue.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A short exchange can be over-emphasized if surfaced without the neighboring watchman and Arabia materials.

primary_reviews.support: The distinct burden title and complete speech exchange justify retrieval when the 21:1-17 parent is also supplied.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No interpretive tradition about Dumah or Seir is available locally to authorize identity claims.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Arabia burden reaches explicit one-year Kedar close
boundary_rationale: Keep 21:13-17 as the Arabia burden with timed Kedar coda because desert lodging, aid, flight, weapons, deadline, and remnant are one compact crisis oracle. Verse 16’s new divine-speech formula sharpens the forecast but does not supersede the burden’s target or create an independent scene.
defensible_basis: The Arabia burden opens with caravans lodging in the thickets, calls Tema to bring water and bread to fugitives, explains flight from warfare, and then gives a hired-worker-like one-year deadline for Kedar’s glory and archers to diminish at 21:17. Splitting at 21:16 detaches the timed verdict from the refugee conditions it answers.

source_observations.text: The burden on Arabia. You will lodge in the thickets in Arabia, you caravans of Dedanites.
and the residue of the number of the archers, the mighty men of the children of Kedar, will be few; for Yahweh, the God of Israel, has spoken it.”

primary_reviews.support: Massa ba’arav governs the caravan and Tema imperatives; ki koh amar at verse 16 supplies a temporal interpretation closed by the YHWH-spoke attestation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The one-year speech is formally distinct and could be indexed as a postscript similar to other timed codas.

primary_reviews.support: Displaced travelers, emergency hospitality, reason for flight, and quantified collapse develop a single desert-refuge scenario to conclusion.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Tema caravans and Kedar warriors are different named groups whose relationship is implied rather than narrated.

primary_reviews.support: Including both aid and deadline keeps humanitarian action beside the war pressure and prevents the forecast from appearing contextless.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The burden remains candidate evidence; historical identification and chronology require sources beyond this local pass.

deciding_marker_or_seam: valley burden reaches oath verdict after the revelry indictment
boundary_rationale: End the valley vision at 22:14 because lament, siege observation, civic response, and revelry indictment culminate in a sworn verdict. The steward oracle following it occupies the same political world but has a fresh addressee and messenger instruction, so it should not be merged merely to fill the chapter.
defensible_basis: The valley-of-vision burden asks why the city has gone to the housetops, laments leaders captured without battle, surveys Elam-Kir assault and breached defenses, and indicts defensive preparations, feasting, and refusal to regard the Maker. The unforgiven-until-death oath closes at 22:14; adding 22:15 would introduce a newly named official and direct commission.

source_observations.text: The burden of the valley of vision. What ails you now, that you have all gone up to the housetops?
Yahweh of Armies revealed himself in my ears, “Surely this iniquity will not be forgiven you until you die,” says the Lord, Yahweh of Armies.

primary_reviews.support: Massa ge-hizzayon opens the address, interrogatives and first-person lament govern its movement, and the revealed oath at verse 14 supplies a formal terminus.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Both this unit and the steward speech concern Jerusalem’s failed leadership and share the chapter setting.

primary_reviews.support: Confused celebration, unseen death, prophetic grief, approaching forces, human fortification, and fatal feasting form a complete city indictment.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The survey of defenses at 22:8-11 and revelry at 12-14 are distinct internal accusation panels.

primary_reviews.support: Keeping the revelry verdict within the burden prevents it from being detached as a generic saying about eating and drinking.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Historical reconstruction may aid context but cannot be treated as local boundary authority.

deciding_marker_or_seam: new official addressee continues through installation and collapsing-peg coda
boundary_rationale: Retain 22:15-25 as the steward deposition-and-installation oracle because the named office and transfer of authority bind its two addressees, while the final peg failure qualifies the installation imagery. The 15-19, 20-24, and 25 children remain serious alternatives, especially if the coda’s attachment receives independent review.
defensible_basis: A messenger command sends the prophet to the steward Shebna, challenges his tomb, announces removal, then shifts at 22:20 to Eliakim’s installation, key, stable peg, household weight, and a collapsing-peg coda at 22:25. Splitting those phases exposes real internal turns but risks separating deposition, replacement, elevation, and warning within one office-transfer oracle.

source_observations.text: The Lord, Yahweh of Armies says, “Go, get yourself to this treasurer, even to Shebna, who is over the house, and say,
“In that day,” says Yahweh of Armies, “the nail that was fastened in a sure place will give way. It will be cut down and fall. The burden that was on it will be cut off, for Yahweh has spoken it.”

primary_reviews.support: A new messenger formula opens at verse 15 and a second in-that-day appointment begins at verse 20, but the final peg saying’s precise antecedent is disputed.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Stewardship, robe, sash, key, peg, and household load connect the removal and replacement movements lexically and institutionally.

primary_reviews.support: Self-made monument, humiliating removal, named successor, transferred insignia, secured authority, accumulated dependents, and collapse make a full reversal sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 20 is a conspicuous new temporal and personal start, while verse 25 can be heard as a separate corrective coda.

primary_reviews.support: Users may need to distinguish the Shebna judgment, Eliakim appointment, and peg-collapse saying rather than receive one composite official oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Separating them can imply independent referents or outcomes that the shared office-transfer parent is designed to constrain.

challenge.claim: The frozen parent may merge three address or image phases whose retrieval questions differ.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Review 22:15-19, 22:20-24, and 22:25 as mandatory-hydration children, preserving uncertainty about the coda’s referent.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Tyre burden and renewed ships lament complete the main oracle
boundary_rationale: Keep 23:1-14 as the principal Tyre lament and divine-purpose oracle because the renewed wail to ships forms an inclusion around its trade-city downfall. The later seventy-year forecast presupposes this loss but changes temporal horizon and rhetorical form, warranting a separate coda child.
defensible_basis: The Tyre burden opens with ships commanded to wail, cycles through coastland, Sidon, Egypt, sea, merchants, divine purpose against pride, and Assyrian ruin, then returns at 23:14 to the opening ship lament. Absorbing 23:15-18 would cross an explicit seventy-year temporal reset and a song-and-profit coda.

source_observations.text: The burden of Tyre. Howl, you ships of Tarshish! For it is laid waste, so that there is no house, no entering in. From the land of Kittim it is revealed to them.
Howl, you ships of Tarshish, for your stronghold is laid waste!

primary_reviews.support: Massa Tsor and the ship-wail imperative begin the burden; the same imperative returns at verse 14 after the divine-purpose and Assyria explanations.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Target and commercial vocabulary continue in verses 15-18, so the coda remains part of the broader Tyre oracle.

primary_reviews.support: Maritime messengers, silenced port, international grief, merchant pride, divine overthrow, and renewed ship lament complete the main elegiac circuit.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Internal voices and geographic shifts make the lament composite even though its refrain unifies it.

primary_reviews.support: The inclusion gives a stronger endpoint than the chapter boundary and keeps trade imagery with the stated anti-pride purpose.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Economic and historical applications lie beyond the boundary task and should not inflate confidence.

deciding_marker_or_seam: explicit seventy-year reset reaches dedicated-profit close
boundary_rationale: Surface 23:15-18 as the seventy-year song and dedicated-profit coda because its temporal frame, quoted song, remembered-city outcome, and consecrated-gain reversal are complete. It remains a child of the Tyre burden, but its opening formula and changed horizon outweigh a chapter-wide flattening.
defensible_basis: An explicit seventy-year transition at 23:15 introduces Tyre’s forgotten interval, a prostitute-song instruction, return to commerce, and the final redirection of profit as dedicated provision at 23:18. Retaining all of chapter 23 would hide this forecast-and-song coda after the main burden’s repeated ship-lament closure.

source_observations.text: It will come to pass in that day that Tyre will be forgotten seventy years, according to the days of one king. After the end of seventy years it will be to Tyre like in the song of the prostitute.

Her merchandise and her wages will be holiness to Yahweh. It will not be treasured nor laid up; for her merchandise will be for those who dwell before Yahweh, to eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing.

primary_reviews.support: Vehayah bayyom hahu plus the numbered period opens the coda; the song imperative and vehayah sequence conclude with qodesh profit language.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Repeated Tyre, commerce, hire, and merchandise terms continue the burden’s subject without a new named heading.

primary_reviews.support: Forgetting, minstrel song, renewed recognition, returned trade, and transformed use of gain create an ironic post-judgment afterpiece.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The coda has limited independence because the reason for forgetting and returning lies in verses 1-14.

primary_reviews.support: Separate retrieval distinguishes downfall from the later commercial reversal while mandatory parent context prevents the latter from sounding like unqualified endorsement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The seventy-year figure remains translation and chronology evidence only, not a seam beyond its explicit local formula.

deciding_marker_or_seam: behold-YHWH-empties opening reaches the emptied-city close
boundary_rationale: End the first world-city judgment tableau at 24:13, where gleaning imagery summarizes what remains after the city’s emptied joy. Verse 14 changes to raised voices and western acclamation, providing a defensible verse-level seam; the entire 24:1-23 chapter remains an alternative if the verse-16 speaker pivot controls retrieval.
defensible_basis: Behold, YHWH empties the earth opens universal leveling, covenant-breaking, curse, withered joy, silenced wine and song, shut houses, desolate city, and an olive-gleaning simile at 24:13. Flattening all of chapter 24 misses the audible turn to distant praise at verse 14, though the later midverse lament complicates finer division.

source_observations.text: Behold, Yahweh makes the earth empty, makes it waste, turns it upside down, and scatters its inhabitants.
For it will be so within the earth among the peoples, as the shaking of an olive tree, as the gleanings when the vintage is done.

primary_reviews.support: Hinneh YHWH opens the devastation; curse and covenant language drive the judgment until olive-beating and post-vintage gleaning provide a terminal remnant simile.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 14’s singing may be an internal response within the same cosmic judgment rather than a new top-level child.

primary_reviews.support: Because the decisive voice reversal occurs inside 24:16 rather than at verse 14, a whole 24:1-23 unit may better respect the poem at verse granularity.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The shift from emptied music to newly raised voices at 24:14 is perceptible and preserves the later complex as a larger held parent.

challenge.claim: The active 24:13 endpoint may anticipate a form break whose strongest pivot is actually intra-verse at 24:16.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Retain 24:1-23 as the coarse verse-granular alternative pending clause-level Hebrew and voice review.

primary_reviews.support: Chapter-scale retrieval may be safer in 24-27 because songs, laments, and cosmic judgment repeatedly interlock across short verse seams.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A 24:1-13 child has a complete desolation-to-gleaning contour and can be hydrated with the entire chapter.

challenge.claim: Finer segmentation of chapter 24 may create apparently independent fragments around a disputed speaker change.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Require chapter-parent hydration and preserve whole-chapter presentation as a nonblocking competing route.

deciding_marker_or_seam: remnant song begins at 14 but the speaker pivots inside verse 16 before fear-pit-snare
boundary_rationale: Hold 24:14-23 as the surfaced parent because its praise-to-lament transition cannot be represented exactly by whole-verse boundaries. The 14-16 plus 17-23 route approximates the shift, while 24:1-23 avoids approximation by staying coarser; neither option may be promoted without independent Hebrew voice and literary adjudication.
rejected_alternative: force a false verse seam at 16 and 17
defensible_basis: Raised western voices begin at 24:14 and spread glory calls eastward, but the speaker turns inside 24:16 from songs of the righteous to personal wasting and treachery; fear-pit-snare, shattered earth, punishment of heavenly and earthly powers, and Zion’s reign then continue through 24:23. A split between verses 16 and 17 would falsely locate a clause-internal pivot at a verse edge.

source_observations.text: These shall lift up their voice. They will shout for the majesty of Yahweh. They cry aloud from the sea.
Then the moon will be confounded, and the sun ashamed; for Yahweh of Armies will reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem; and glory will be before his elders.

hold.question: Should 24:14-23 surface as 14-16 and 17-23, or remain whole because the decisive lament pivot occurs inside verse 16?
options: surface 24:14-16 and 24:17-23 with explicit midverse approximation disclosure
retain 24:14-23 as the only surfaced unit
hold.requested_reviewer: independent Hebrew discourse and poetic-voice specialist plus human/external-AI adjudicator

primary_reviews.support: The first-person lament begins after praise within verse 16, and the available OSHB/UXLC WLC-family evidence cannot turn that clause seam into an exact verse boundary.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Fear, pit, and snare clearly launch a new judgment sequence at verse 17 even if the emotional pivot starts earlier.

primary_reviews.support: Praise in 14-16 and terror-to-enthronement in 17-23 are recognizable movements, but the lament’s intra-verse entrance makes a clean child split impossible in the current address model.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Retaining 14-23 preserves all voices but under-exposes the real praise, lament, and cosmic judgment changes.

challenge.claim: The frozen larger unit sacrifices literary precision to verse-address precision.

deciding_marker_or_seam: YHWH-my-God praise reaches silencing of the ruthless

deciding_marker_or_seam: introduced strong-city song reaches trampling by poor feet

deciding_marker_or_seam: path-of-the-just reset reaches fire-for-adversaries close

deciding_marker_or_seam: Ariel הוי reaches dreamlike enemy dissolution
