Verse 9 introduces new imperatives to pause and become blind. The 29:1-14 merger preserves perception imagery but loses on audience and rhetorical form.
defensible_basis: The doubled Ariel woe at 29:1 opens a siege oracle; low speech, sudden visitation, and enemy dissolution culminate in the hungry-and-thirsty dream comparison at 29:8. Adding 29:9-14 crosses from the dreamlike fate of Ariel's attackers to self-blinding commands and a sealed-document dispute after the named-city form has reached its exact dream endpoint.

source_observations.text: Woe to Ariel! Ariel, the city where David encamped! Add year to year; let the feasts come around;

It will be like when a hungry man dreams, and behold, he eats; but he awakes, and his hunger isn’t satisfied; or like when a thirsty man dreams, and behold, he drinks; but he awakes, and behold, he is faint, and he is still thirsty. The multitude of all the nations that fight against Mount Zion will be like that.

primary_reviews.support: The woe and repeated Ariel vocative define scope, while enemy and dream vocabulary converge in verses 7-8 before plural imperatives restart.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Drunkenness at 29:9 echoes the preceding altered-perception imagery and forms a lexical bridge into the next panel.

primary_reviews.support: Annual feasts become siege, low speech, sudden reversal, and a doubled night-dream simile, giving the named-city oracle closure.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Deep sleep in 29:10 continues the dream motif, making 29:1-14 a plausible macro movement despite the local seam.

primary_reviews.support: Zion or Ariel relations elsewhere do not decide the endpoint; the local named-city and dream frame supplies the candidate evidence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Users may need 29:9-14 to see unread vision follow the siege dream, so parent hydration remains advisable.

deciding_marker_or_seam: bewilderment imperatives reach wonder-upon-wonder verdict
boundary_rationale: Surface the sealed-document disputation from its bewilderment imperatives to the loss of wise understanding at 29:14. Demonstration, diagnosis, and verdict are all present. Verse 15 begins a fresh hidden-counsel woe, while verses 1-8 concern Ariel's attackers; neither neighboring form should absorb this bounded exchange.
defensible_basis: Commands to pause, wonder, and become blind at 29:9 open a stupefaction discourse; deep sleep, covered seers, two failed readings of a sealed document, and the lip-versus-heart charge reach the wonder-upon-wonder verdict at 29:14. Retaining 29:1-14 subordinates this demonstration to Ariel's already-resolved siege dream.

source_observations.text: Pause and wonder! Blind yourselves and be blind! They are drunken, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink.

therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvelous work among this people, even a marvelous work and a wonder; and the wisdom of their wise men will perish, and the understanding of their prudent men will be hidden.”

primary_reviews.support: Plural imperatives initiate the passage, vision and document diction govern its middle, and the causal announcement resolves it in verse 14.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Deep-sleep language connects backward to the dream in 29:7-8, so the opening is an intensification within a larger cycle.

primary_reviews.support: Two miniature reading scenes embody blindness, and the direct speech in 29:13-14 interprets them and closes the form.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The sealed book can elaborate the preceding night vision, supporting 29:1-14 as a parent even though not as the child.

primary_reviews.support: Citation pressure on 29:13 can detach the lip-heart charge from both the sealed book and its announced consequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The selected span includes the demonstrations before the charge and the verdict after it, preventing the narrowest extraction.

challenge.claim: Retrieval may still return only 29:13-14.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Index 29:9-14 as the minimum surfaced object and forbid a quotation-sized child.

deciding_marker_or_seam: new hidden-counsel הוי reaches potter-Lebanon-Jacob reversal
boundary_rationale: Retain the hidden-counsel and Jacob-reversal oracle through the erring-to-understanding close at 29:24. The woe and potter image define what the subsequent transformation corrects. A 29:17-24 child loses that governing accusation, and 29:9-24 masks the fresh woe that changes the issue from unread vision to concealed counsel.
defensible_basis: A new hidden-counsel woe starts at 29:15; the potter-clay rebuke turns at 29:17 into Lebanon transformation, restored senses, removed oppressors, and Jacob's passage from shame to sanctifying and instruction, ending at 29:24. Splitting at verse 17 divides accusation from reversal, while merging backward ignores the explicit woe after the sealed-book verdict.

source_observations.text: Woe to those who deeply hide their counsel from Yahweh, and whose deeds are in the dark, and who say, “Who sees us?” and “Who knows us?”
They also who err in spirit will come to understanding, and those who grumble will receive instruction.”

primary_reviews.support: The woe particle opens, a temporal question pivots at 29:17, and paired instruction clauses complete the reversal in verse 24.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Blindness-to-sight imagery continues 29:9-14, producing meaningful cohesion across verse 15 despite the reset.

primary_reviews.support: Hidden deeds and inverted potter logic yield to transformed land, senses, justice, and household response in one reversal arc.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verses 17-24 can resemble a separate salvation poem, but without 15-16 they lose the inversion being answered.

primary_reviews.support: Other potter or deaf-blind passages illuminate imagery but cannot establish the 29:15 or 29:17 seam.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The unit contains several reusable motifs, so retrieval should preserve its woe-to-reversal logic rather than return only promise.

deciding_marker_or_seam: rebellious-children הוי reaches Rahab-sits-still verdict
boundary_rationale: Surface the Egypt-alliance woe and Rahab taunt from its accusation to the naming endpoint at 30:7. Policy, journey, envoys, animals, and the no-profit verdict share one target. Verse 8 starts a durable written record for a new accusation panel, so 30:1-17 loses as a coarse aggregate despite audience continuity.
defensible_basis: The rebellious-children woe at 30:1 indicts counsel and alliance apart from Yahweh; descent to Egypt, Pharaoh confidence, envoy itinerary, and the animal burden converge on the Rahab-who-sits-still verdict at 30:7. Extending through 30:17 crosses the command to inscribe a witness at verse 8, while detaching 30:6-7 loses the caravan's alliance function.

source_observations.text: “Woe to the rebellious children”, says Yahweh, “who take counsel, but not from me; and who make an alliance, but not with my Spirit, that they may add sin to sin;
For Egypt helps in vain, and to no purpose; therefore I have called her Rahab who sits still.

primary_reviews.support: Woe and participial accusations govern the Egypt descent, and the naming clause at 30:7 turns no-profit diction into a closing taunt.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The rebellious audience reappears in 30:9, giving real continuity across the writing command at the chosen endpoint.

primary_reviews.support: Policy, journey, diplomatic stops, burdened beasts, and the motionless Rahab nickname create a coherent anti-alliance satire.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The tablet records the same refusal and failed flight, so the two children need a shared chapter-cycle parent.

primary_reviews.support: Egypt and exodus relations cannot create the boundary; local counsel, journey, and naming functions are the relevant evidence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A narrow reading could overgeneralize Rahab without the precise political-literary setting supplied by all seven verses.

deciding_marker_or_seam: writing command reaches failed-flight reversal
boundary_rationale: Choose the inscribed-witness and failed-flight oracle through the mountain-beacon endpoint at 30:17. Written charge, quoted rejection, divine answer, and consequence form a complete evidentiary movement. The 30:1-17 alternative is thematically broad but formally coarse, and a verse-15 child misrepresents the text by omitting 'You refused.'
defensible_basis: The tablet-and-book command at 30:8 establishes a witness; anti-prophetic demands receive a wall and shattered-pot verdict, an offered rest is explicitly refused, and flight ends with a solitary beacon at 30:17. Isolating 30:15 severs offer from refusal, while attaching 30:1-7 folds a new documentary act into the completed Rahab taunt.

source_observations.text: Now go, write it before them on a tablet, and inscribe it in a book, that it may be for the time to come forever and ever.
One thousand will flee at the threat of one. At the threat of five, you will flee until you are left like a beacon on the top of a mountain, and like a banner on a hill.

primary_reviews.support: Write and inscribe imperatives mark a new act; quotation, causal response, and flee/swift wordplay reach the remnant similes in 30:17.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The title 'rebellious children' repeats 30:1's audience, so the inscription remains connected to the preceding policy indictment.

primary_reviews.support: Record, demands, collapsing wall, broken vessel, rest, horses, pursuit, and lonely signal enact one written warning.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The Egypt policy explains the choice to flee on horses, making previous-sibling context essential even with a valid seam.

primary_reviews.support: Quietness and confidence in verse 15 attract isolated retrieval, and 30:1-17 would offer maximum protection against it.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The frozen ten-verse span already contains accusation, offer, refusal, and result; the Rahab caravan is not required to cure that distortion.

challenge.claim: Systems may return only the positive half of 30:15.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Make 30:8-17 indivisible for quotation and hydrate it with 30:1-7.

deciding_marker_or_seam: therefore reversal reaches healing and transformed-light close
boundary_rationale: Retain the waiting-grace, way, and healing poem from its blessed-waiting opening to Yahweh binding the fracture at 30:26. The Assyria-theophany alternative through verse 33 loses because 30:27 begins a new behold announcement, changes affect and target, and replaces restoration imagery with an approaching fiery judgment.
defensible_basis: The double therefore at 30:18 reverses failed flight into waiting grace; answered cry, visible teachers, guiding voice, discarded images, abundance, water, transformed light, and healed wounds culminate at 30:26. Merging 30:27-33 crosses from consolation to fiery arrival, while extending backward overlooks the explicit mercy reset.

source_observations.text: Therefore Yahweh will wait, that he may be gracious to you; and therefore he will be exalted, that he may have mercy on you, for Yahweh is a God of justice. Blessed are all those who wait for him.

Moreover the light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be seven times brighter, like the light of seven days, in the day that Yahweh binds up the fracture of his people, and heals the wound they were struck with.

primary_reviews.support: The adversative turn at 30:18 inaugurates mercy; second-person promises accumulate until binding and healing verbs close verse 26.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Slaughter and transformed light in 30:25-26 can anticipate the fiery arrival at 30:27 within a larger theophany sequence.

primary_reviews.support: Waiting, hearing, seeing, walking, discarding, sowing, watering, illuminating, binding, and healing trace a coherent restoration progression.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Violent background imagery means the seam is formal, not a simple thematic division between grace and judgment.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical echoes of teacher, way, light, or healing cannot fix the 30:18 or 30:26 coordinates.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Standalone promise retrieval may flatten the poem unless failed flight and divine arrival remain available as adjacent context.

deciding_marker_or_seam: behold-name-of-YHWH reset reaches prepared pyre close
boundary_rationale: Surface the divine-name arrival and Topheth oracle through the sulfurous-breath endpoint at 30:33. Its bodily and acoustic imagery forms one advance from distance to prepared fire. The 30:18-33 alternative preserves a broad cycle but loses at 30:27's deictic restart after the preceding poem has already concluded in healing.
defensible_basis: The behold announcement at 30:27 presents Yahweh's name arriving from afar; lips, tongue, breath, voice, arm, and rod drive the advance until divine breath kindles the prepared burning place at 30:33. Absorbing 30:18-26 crosses its healed-wound closure, while cutting before the pyre leaves the announced arrival without its exact destination.

source_observations.text: Behold, Yahweh’s name comes from far away, burning with his anger, and in thick rising smoke. His lips are full of indignation. His tongue is as a devouring fire.
For his burning place has long been ready. Yes, it is prepared for the king. He has made its pyre deep and large with fire and much wood. Yahweh’s breath, like a stream of sulfur, kindles it.

primary_reviews.support: A behold construction opens a new scene, and repeated bodily and sound terms culminate in the breath that ignites the pyre.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Day, light, and fire vocabulary connects backward to 30:18-26, confirming that both children inhabit one chapter movement.

primary_reviews.support: Approach, sifting, song, audible battle, rod strokes, and burning place create a complete theophanic progression.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The festival song in verse 29 recalls blessing and serves as an internal bridge rather than a total break.

primary_reviews.support: Assyria and Topheth relations elsewhere cannot dictate this seam, and the king reference cannot settle identity or chronology.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Dense violent imagery without 30:18-26 could conceal the chapter's mercy movement, so a parent remains operationally necessary.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Egypt-help הוי reaches defending imagery return call and divine-fire close
boundary_rationale: Keep the Egypt-help woe and defending oracle through its furnace-in-Jerusalem endpoint at 31:9. The accusation receives linked answers and a formal closing formula. A cross-chapter 31:1-32:8 parent is useful, but the new king-and-princes presentation changes subject and mode after chapter 31 has already closed.
defensible_basis: The Egypt-help woe at 31:1 contrasts horses and chariots with seeking Yahweh; flesh-versus-spirit, lion and bird protection, return, discarded idols, and Assyria's nonhuman sword reach the says-Yahweh close about Zion's fire at 31:9. Merging 32:1-8 crosses into a fresh behold announcement of righteous rule.

source_observations.text: Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, and rely on horses, and trust in chariots because they are many, and in horsemen because they are very strong, but they don’t look to the Holy One of Israel, and they don’t seek Yahweh!
His rock will pass away by reason of terror, and his princes will be afraid of the banner,” says Yahweh, whose fire is in Zion, and his furnace in Jerusalem.

primary_reviews.support: A woe particle initiates the indictment, imperatives and similes develop its answer, and the final oracle formula terminates the Assyria panel.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The righteous ruler at 32:1 can function as a positive answer to failed human reliance across the chapter seam.

primary_reviews.support: Misplaced trust, simultaneous collapse, defended Zion, return, idol rejection, Assyrian fall, and furnace form a full progression.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The protection horizon continues naturally into 32:1-8, so next-sibling context should remain available.

primary_reviews.support: A 31:1-32:8 parent would keep the critique of human help beside the just-rule contrast.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The selected chapter contains accusation, protection, return, and closure without requiring a ruler-identity decision.

challenge.claim: Ending at 31:9 may hide the adjacent governance answer.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Preserve a cross-chapter parent over the two form-specific children.

deciding_marker_or_seam: behold-a-king reset reaches noble-villain contrast
boundary_rationale: Accept the righteous-ruler and character-contrast form from 32:1 through the noble-versus-scoundrel close at 32:8. Verse 9 replaces descriptive maxims with direct imperatives to women at ease. The 31:1-32:8 alternative remains a parent but loses at the behold reset and cannot authorize royal identity.
defensible_basis: The behold announcement at 32:1 presents a king and princes ruling justly; shelter, opened senses, clear speech, and fool-scoundrel character exposure end with the noble person's conduct at 32:8. Identifying the ruler exceeds boundary evidence, and merger with chapter 31 ignores this fresh presentation and the exact character-contrast endpoint.

source_observations.text: Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness, and princes shall rule in justice.
But the noble devises noble things, and he will continue in noble things.

primary_reviews.support: The presentational particle and rule verbs introduce the scene; fool, scoundrel, and noble diction creates an antithetical close at verse 8.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No messenger formula marks the chapter boundary, and just rule can answer the preceding Zion-defense oracle.

primary_reviews.support: Governance unfolds through shelter, perception, speech, naming, conduct, and a final character contrast before a new audience appears.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: These maxims could sit inside a larger restoration poem, but verse 9 still supplies a durable local turn.

primary_reviews.support: Later royal or shelter imagery cannot identify the king or determine this boundary; immediate form is the available basis.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Independent presentation may invite identity claims, so non-authorizing metadata must remain explicit.

deciding_marker_or_seam: women vocative reaches spirit transformation and blessed sowing
boundary_rationale: Retain the women-lament and spirit-transformation movement from its audience call to the sowing blessing at 32:20. The lament-to-promise turn at verse 15 is a valid internal seam, but loses as an independent boundary because each half states the other's function through 'until'; the larger child preserves the complete reversal.
defensible_basis: Commands to rise, hear, tremble, strip, and mourn address women at ease in 32:9-12; failed harvest and abandoned city persist until spirit is poured from on high at 32:15, then justice, peace, security, leveling, and blessed sowing close at 32:20. Splitting promise from lament severs the grammatical until-hinge and its transformation.

source_observations.text: Rise up, you women who are at ease! Hear my voice! You careless daughters, give ear to my speech!
Blessed are you who sow beside all waters, who send out the feet of the ox and the donkey.

primary_reviews.support: Feminine plural imperatives fix the audience, and the temporal construction at 32:15 carries desolation into the poured-spirit reversal.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The form shift from lament commands to future restoration is strong enough to support internal indexing under mandatory hydration.

primary_reviews.support: Failed vintage, exposed mourning, deserted city, transformed terrain, resident justice, peace, safety, and sowing form a loss-to-renewal arc.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The sudden hail-and-city line in verse 19 complicates a smooth restoration reading of the closing panel.

primary_reviews.support: The poured-spirit portion attracts extraction, and a direct internal locator could aid retrieval.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Standalone extraction would erase the explicit until relation; the frozen unit safely binds condition and reversal.

challenge.claim: Users may need focused access to 32:15-20.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Provide an internal locator with compulsory 32:9-20 parent hydration.

deciding_marker_or_seam: destroyer הוי and communal plea reach stability-and-treasure close
boundary_rationale: Surface the destroyer-woe and supplication through the stability-and-treasure endpoint at 33:6. The singular accusation and plural prayer are responsive parts of one compact movement. The chapter-sized alternative loses when 'Behold, their valiant ones cry' starts a new crisis report before a distinct divine answer.
defensible_basis: The destroyer woe at 33:1 is answered by a communal grace plea; scattering, plunder, Yahweh's exaltation, and Zion's justice culminate in stability, salvation, wisdom, knowledge, and fear as treasure at 33:6. A whole-chapter unit crosses the fresh envoy lament at 33:7 and suppresses later response and city-vision forms.

source_observations.text: Woe to you who destroy, but you weren’t destroyed, and who betray, but nobody betrayed you! When you have finished destroying, you will be destroyed; and when you have finished betrayal, you will be betrayed.
There will be stability in your times, abundance of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge. The fear of Yahweh is your treasure.

primary_reviews.support: Woe opens as accusation, first-person plural plea follows, and nominal clauses of exaltation and stability close before a deictic reset.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The unnamed destroyer and communal plea could form the opening stanza of a longer chapter liturgy.

primary_reviews.support: Threat, prayer, scattering, plunder, exalted rule, and durable treasure create a mini-cycle that changes scene at the envoys.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Chapter 33 repeatedly alternates crisis and assurance, so 33:1-24 remains an important macro composition.

primary_reviews.support: No external relation fixes the 33:6/7 seam; local woe, prayer, and crisis-report transition are decisive evidence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Returning verses 1-6 alone can detach the stability assurance from the acute breakdown narrated next.

deciding_marker_or_seam: fresh envoy lament reaches divine rising and sinner question-answer
boundary_rationale: Keep the crisis lament, divine response, and dwellers answer from 33:7 to the bread-and-water endpoint at 33:16. defensible_basis: The behold report at 33:7 introduces crying valiant ones and peace envoys; deserted roads and mourning land lead to Yahweh's triple-now response, burning judgment, a far-and-near summons, and the sinners' question answered by the secure righteous dweller at 33:16. Merging the future city vision crosses the 'Your eyes will see' reset at verse 17.

source_observations.text: Behold, their valiant ones cry outside; the ambassadors of peace weep bitterly.
he will dwell on high. His place of defense will be the fortress of rocks. His bread will be supplied. His waters will be sure.

primary_reviews.support: A new deictic report begins, repeated 'now' marks the divine answer, and question-answer syntax closes with secure provision.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The dwell-on-high promise flows into seeing the king at 33:17, so the seam divides closely linked assurances.

primary_reviews.support: Envoy grief broadens to land lament, intervention, summons, fearful inquiry, and a portrait of the secure dweller.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: That portrait may continue into the city vision, especially because both panels describe security rather than a new historical scene.

primary_reviews.support: The answer to who can dwell is vulnerable to moralizing extraction if separated from the gracious city vision.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The frozen span includes crisis, divine response, question, and answer; parent hydration can supply the following prospect.

deciding_marker_or_seam: eyes-will-see-a-king reset reaches healed and forgiven close
boundary_rationale: Accept the king-and-city vision from the seeing promise through the healed-and-forgiven population close at 33:24. Perception, memory, Zion, rivers, acclamation, ship contrast, and communal resolution form one prospect. defensible_basis: The promise to see the king in beauty at 33:17 opens a future city vision; remembered terror yields to an immovable Zion tent, majestic waters, a judge-lawgiver-king acclamation, disabled rigging, plunder, and inhabitants healed and forgiven at 33:24. Isolating the final verse loses the tableau that gives sickness and pardon their setting.

source_observations.text: Your eyes will see the king in his beauty. They will see a distant land.
The inhabitant won’t say, “I am sick.” The people who dwell therein will be forgiven their iniquity.

primary_reviews.support: Second-person future perception opens, Zion language organizes the scene, and the final negative speech plus forgiveness clause supplies closure.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Secure dwelling in 33:16 is a natural antecedent, so verse 17 is a presentation shift rather than an absolute break.

primary_reviews.support: Beauty, vanished terror, stable tent, broad waters, royal acclamation, failed ship, plunder, healing, and pardon compose a resolved vision.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Broken rigging in 33:23 interrupts serenity and may reach back toward the crisis sequence.

primary_reviews.support: Keeping verse 24 with the full city scene resists extracting healing or forgiveness and preserves the threefold acclamation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Royal and Zion relations may invite identity claims; those connections remain context evidence, not boundary or theology authority.

deciding_marker_or_seam: nations summons reaches measured land-possession close
boundary_rationale: Retain the nations-Edom judgment and land register through the generational-dwelling endpoint at 34:17. The 34-35 alternative remains a diptych parent and loses as a child when 35:1 changes subject and mode to wilderness rejoicing.

defensible_basis: The nations-and-earth summons at 34:1 opens judgment that narrows from cosmic dissolution to Edom and Bozrah, then land-burning, animal habitation, a book-search command, and allotted possession ending at 34:17. Splitting at rare diction in 34:5 or textual pressure in 34:16 breaks the land register; a 34-35 megaunit erases chapter 35's new rejoicing form.

source_observations.text: Come near, you nations, to hear! Listen, you peoples. Let the earth and all it contains hear, the world, and everything that comes from it.
He has cast the lot for them, and his hand has divided it to them with a measuring line. They shall possess it forever. From generation to generation they will dwell in it.

primary_reviews.support: Hearing imperatives and final lot-and-line allocation bracket the chapter, while WLC-family wording supports register continuity.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The syntax and speaker of 34:16 are difficult, and OSHB with UXLC cannot independently select a rendering or local voice.

primary_reviews.support: Universal summons narrows to a named land, transforms it, inventories inhabitants, and seals possession in one oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The turn from slaughter to animals could support internal children, though both panels depend on the land's reversal.

primary_reviews.support: Reading chapters 34-35 together protects the ruined-versus-blossoming wilderness contrast.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A macro parent preserves the contrast while each chapter retains its summons, participants, imagery, and close.

challenge.claim: Independent chapter 34 retrieval may hide the restoration mirror.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Require the 34:1-35:10 diptych parent and next sibling.

deciding_marker_or_seam: desert rejoicing reaches redeemed-return refrain
boundary_rationale: Surface the wilderness-restoration and Holy Way poem from desert rejoicing to the ransomed return at 35:10. Landscape, bodies, water, road, safety, and joyful arrival form one procession. Chapter 34 remains contrastive parent context but loses as part of a single active child after its allotted ruin has already closed.
defensible_basis: Wilderness and desert become rejoicing, blossoming subjects at 35:1-2; commands strengthen weak bodies, divine arrival opens senses, waters change the land, and the Holy Way carries the redeemed until sorrow flees at 35:10. A 34-35 megaunit suppresses the restoration form, while fragmenting bodies or highway severs transformation from the return refrain.

source_observations.text: The wilderness and the dry land will be glad. The desert will rejoice and blossom like a rose.
Then Yahweh’s ransomed ones will return, and come with singing to Zion; and everlasting joy will be on their heads. They will obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing will flee away.”

primary_reviews.support: Feminine landscape subjects and joy verbs open, imperatives and future changes sustain, and return-with-singing closes verse 10.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No formal heading separates 35:1, and shared desert and animal imagery deliberately binds the two chapters.

primary_reviews.support: Blossoming land, strengthened people, opened senses, water, designated road, absent predators, and arrival form a complete poem.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its force depends on reversing chapter 34, so standalone presentation cannot treat it as context-free promise.

primary_reviews.support: Later reuse can pull 35:3-6 or 35:8-10 out of both the poem and its diptych setting.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The whole-chapter child prevents narrower fragmentation, and parent hydration resolves the remaining contrast risk.

challenge.claim: The complete poem can still be surfaced without Isaiah 34.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Attach the 34:1-35:10 parent and previous sibling.

deciding_marker_or_seam: dated arrival and public challenge reach commanded-silence close
boundary_rationale: Keep the dated siege-embassy narrative from arrival through the delegation's return-and-report endpoint at 36:22. The extension to 37:7 gains causal continuity but loses scene integrity: hearing, sackcloth, temple entry, a newly sent party, and Isaiah's reply form the next episode under the same historical parent.
defensible_basis: The dated regnal frame at 36:1 opens Sennacherib's campaign and the Rabshakeh embassy; location, officials, language negotiation, public challenge, commanded silence, and the torn-clothes report resolve the scene at 36:22. Crossing into 37:1-7 merges this completed confrontation with Hezekiah's new temple movement and consultation.

source_observations.text: Now in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked all of the fortified cities of Judah and captured them.

Then Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah, the son of Asaph the recorder, came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn, and told him the words of Rabshakeh.

primary_reviews.support: Wayyiqtol progression, the Aramaic-versus-Judahite exchange, and final reporting verb carry one prose scene from dispatch to return.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The report remains unanswered until 37:1, so the narrative macro-scene plainly continues across the chapter boundary.

primary_reviews.support: Embassy arrival, first challenge, language dispute, public challenge, silence, and exit form a staged confrontation.

primary_reviews.support: Parallel historical material and immediate continuation favor a larger 36:1-37:7 hydration object.

source_observations.text: “Come down and sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon. Sit on the ground without a throne, daughter of the Chaldeans. For you will no longer be called tender and delicate.
The things that you labored in will be like this: those who have trafficked with you from your youth will each wander in his own way. There will be no one to save you.

primary_reviews.support: Second-feminine imperatives and accusations sustain the daughter-city address from the dust command through the no-savior conclusion.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The discourse marker at 47:8 is substantial and could support literary children even though the Hebrew addressee continues.

primary_reviews.support: The literary primary treats 47:1-7 as dethronement and 47:8-15 as a complacency indictment with an expert catalogue.

primary_reviews.support: Later Babylon taunts may echo this poem, but those relations cannot decide whether verse 8 is an active seam.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Reception history creates a risk of reading later city imagery back into Isaiah's unit structure.

deciding_marker_or_seam: hear-this opening reaches for-my-own-sake close
boundary_rationale: Accept 48:1-11 as the indictment-and-refinement movement. Its final concern is the divine name and glory, not the speaker puzzle of verse 16; treating all of chapter 48 as one chunk would bury the explicit readdress at 48:12.
defensible_basis: The 'hear this, house of Jacob' summons opens a long accusation about false naming, foretelling, obstinacy, and refining. The repeated 'for my sake' rationale in verse 11 completes that defense before a second listen command changes the speech at verse 12.

source_observations.text: “Hear this, house of Jacob, you who are called by the name of Israel, and have come out of the waters of Judah. You swear by Yahweh’s name, and make mention of the God of Israel, but not in truth, nor in righteousness—
For my own sake, for my own sake, I will do it; for how would my name be profaned? I will not give my glory to another.

primary_reviews.support: The initial shim'u-zot governs accusations and first-person explanations through the doubled self-sake statement of verse 11.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Internal paragraph marks and changes from accusation to disclosure occur within 1-11, but none supplies a stronger close than verse 11.

primary_reviews.support: An addressed indictment moves from hypocritical naming through prior prediction to the refining explanation, then ends on withheld glory.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verses 6-8 introduce 'new things' and could be overread as a separate oracle rather than an internal evidentiary panel.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical discussions of foreknowledge and refining do not furnish an independent literary seam for Isaiah 48.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The chapter's later departure command is relevant context and must remain linked through the 46-48 parent.

deciding_marker_or_seam: listen-to-me reset reaches syntactically difficult sent-speaker statement
boundary_rationale: Accept 48:12-16 provisionally as the complete listen-and-sent-speaker movement. The next verse begins a clear redeemer formula, whereas splitting verse 16 to force an identity solution would make the chunk map perform exegesis it is not authorized to decide.
defensible_basis: The renewed 'listen to me, Jacob and Israel' at verse 12 starts a creator-and-agent address, but verse 16 ends with a difficult first-person claim about being sent. That syntactic pressure is preserved inside this medium-confidence unit rather than resolved by naming the speaker.

source_observations.text: “Listen to me, O Jacob, and Israel my called: I am he. I am the first. I am also the last.
“Come near to me and hear this: “From the beginning I have not spoken in secret; from the time that it happened, I was there.” Now the Lord Yahweh has sent me with his Spirit.

primary_reviews.support: The plural approach-and-hear imperatives in 48:16 and the clause 'now the Lord YHWH has sent me' introduce a real speaker-assignment difficulty.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The fresh listen command at 48:12 and redeemer formula at 48:17 still provide defensible outer bounds.

challenge.claim: The discourse identity and attachment of the final clause in 48:16 remain unresolved.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Retain 48:12-16 at medium confidence and obtain direct Hebrew discourse review before any smaller child is surfaced.

primary_reviews.support: Creator assertions, the chosen agent, the call to draw near, and the sent-speaker statement make a compact but deliberately ambiguous address.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 16 contains an internal turn that a clause-level model could represent more precisely than the present verse-granular route.

primary_reviews.support: Other canonical speaker and sending texts cannot identify the voice here or manufacture a boundary inside verse 16.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Cross-references may increase interpretive pressure precisely where the local syntax remains unsettled.

deciding_marker_or_seam: redeemer formula reaches Babylon departure and no-peace refrain
boundary_rationale: Accept 48:17-22 as a teaching and departure oracle. Verse 20 belongs with the command, announced proclamation, and water-from-rock sequence; isolating the famous exit line would strip away both its introduction and its no-peace coda.
defensible_basis: The redeemer-and-Holy-One formula at 48:17 changes the mode to teaching, lament over missed obedience, and an imperative departure from Babylon. The exodus-like report culminates in the no-peace refrain at verse 22, which closes the chapter's final movement.

source_observations.text: Yahweh, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, says: “I am Yahweh your God, who teaches you to profit, who leads you by the way that you should go.
“There is no peace”, says Yahweh, “for the wicked.”

primary_reviews.support: A new koh-amar formula names redeemer and teacher at 48:17, while the exodus imperatives and no-peace saying carry the speech to verse 22.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 20 is marked by plural imperatives and can function as an internal proclamation panel.

primary_reviews.support: Instruction, counterfactual lament, departure summons, travel provision, and refrain make one deliberately varied closing oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The no-peace line could be treated as a floating refrain, but here it functions as the chapter's explicit coda.

primary_reviews.support: Exodus relations illuminate the departure imagery without independently selecting verse 20 or 22 as a retrieval seam.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Extracting the Babylon command through later reuse could hide the preceding teacher-and-way frame.

deciding_marker_or_seam: coastlands listen opens call testimony and enlarged mission
boundary_rationale: Accept 49:1-6 as a servant-call and mission unit without deciding who the speaker is. The formal response at verse 7 creates the next seam; an identity-based split inside 1-6 would confuse a contested referent with observable literary form.
defensible_basis: The coastlands imperative opens a first-person call testimony: womb naming, weapon images, reported commission, lament, and an enlarged mission. Verse 6 finishes that commissioning dialogue at the end of the earth before a new divine formula addresses the despised figure.

source_observations.text: Listen, islands, to me. Listen, you peoples, from afar: Yahweh has called me from the womb; from the inside of my mother, he has mentioned my name.

Indeed, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel. I will also give you as a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

primary_reviews.support: Plural coastlands commands, first-person perfects, embedded divine speech, and the culminating mission infinitive form a complete testimony.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The referent of 'Israel' in verse 3 and the return language in verses 5-6 remain translation and identity hot zones.

primary_reviews.support: Call report, vocational imagery, complaint, answer, and expanded commission trace a recognizable prophetic testimony arc.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The internal speech shifts at verses 3 and 5 are real but remain parts of one recounted commissioning event.

primary_reviews.support: Later quotations of the light-to-nations line demonstrate relation, not an Isaiah seam or an identity verdict.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Famous-line retrieval could sever verse 6 from the failure-and-answer sequence that gives it literary force.

deciding_marker_or_seam: new thus-says address reaches creation-praise close
boundary_rationale: Accept 49:7-13 as the response to the preceding call testimony. Keeping the cosmic praise with the promise prevents a split between announced restoration and its formal acclamation, while the Zion complaint at verse 14 unmistakably opens another voice.
defensible_basis: The redeemer formula at verse 7 begins a response promising recognition, restoration, release, provision, and return; heaven, earth, and mountains answer with praise in verse 13. That hymnic close completes the response rather than merely decorating it.

source_observations.text: Yahweh, the Redeemer of Israel, and his Holy One, says to him whom man despises, to him whom the nation abhors, to a servant of rulers: “Kings shall see and rise up, princes, and they shall worship, because of Yahweh who is faithful, even the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you.”
Sing, heavens, and be joyful, earth! Break out into singing, mountains! For Yahweh has comforted his people, and will have compassion on his afflicted.

primary_reviews.support: Koh-amar at 49:7 resets the address, and the imperative cosmic praise at verse 13 marks a completed response before 'Zion said.'
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Several promise panels have paragraph-level interest, but no internal formula displaces the full response-and-hymn frame.

primary_reviews.support: Royal recognition, covenant restoration, prisoner release, pastoral provision, gathering, and creation praise rise as one answer sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verses 8-12 could be indexed as promise subpanels only if their dependence on the response formula remains explicit.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical reuse of individual restoration lines cannot determine whether the poem should be subdivided for retrieval.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The 49:1-13 macro-parent remains important because the response presupposes the servant testimony.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Zion-said complaint reaches astonished child-count question
boundary_rationale: Accept 49:14-21 as Zion's complaint and maternal-children answer. Verse 22 introduces a fresh divine formula and a nations-standard scene, so merging that panel would mute the carefully staged movement from private lament to astonished recognition.
defensible_basis: 'Zion said' gives verse 14 a new speaker and complaint; the answer uses maternal memory, engraved walls, returning children, and a series of astonished questions. The final 'who has brought up these?' question at verse 21 completes the abandoned-to-overfull reversal.

source_observations.text: But Zion said, “Yahweh has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me.”

Then you will say in your heart, ‘Who has conceived these for me, since I have been bereaved of my children and am alone, an exile, and wandering back and forth? Who has brought these up? Behold, I was left alone. Where were these?’”

primary_reviews.support: The reporting clause 'Zion said' opens a complaint-answer exchange, and the interrogatives of verses 20-21 finish its child-count tableau.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The answer continues thematically into the nations' return of children in verses 22-23.

primary_reviews.support: A single voiced complaint is answered through maternal comparison and the visible arrival of children, ending in astonishment rather than decree.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The boundary is relationally porous because the next unit explains how those children are carried back.

primary_reviews.support: The premortem warns that 49:14-50:3 may require strong hydration across Zion, children, captors, and the divorce-creditor disputation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The explicit voice and formula changes still justify local children under that cross-chapter parent.

challenge.claim: Independent retrieval of 49:14-21 may weaken the argument continuing through 50:3.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Require 49:14-50:3 hydration whenever this complaint-answer child is surfaced.

deciding_marker_or_seam: fresh divine formula reaches all-flesh recognition
boundary_rationale: Accept 49:22-26 as the nations-standard and captor-deliverance panel. Its question and answer must remain together; atomizing verses 24-26 would produce a query without its rebuttal and detach the recognition statement from the rescue.
defensible_basis: A new 'thus says the Lord YHWH' at verse 22 raises a signal to nations, depicts children carried home, and answers whether captives can be taken from the mighty. The all-flesh recognition formula at verse 26 supplies a categorical close.

source_observations.text: The Lord Yahweh says, “Behold, I will lift up my hand to the nations, and lift up my banner to the peoples. They shall bring your sons in their bosom, and your daughters shall be carried on their shoulders.

I will feed those who oppress you with their own flesh; and they will be drunk on their own blood, as with sweet wine. Then all flesh shall know that I, Yahweh, am your Savior and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob.”

primary_reviews.support: The messenger formula and hand-signal imagery restart the speech, while the captive question is answered through the all-flesh conclusion.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verses 22-23 also complete the child-return imagery begun in Zion's preceding complaint.

primary_reviews.support: Nations procession, royal fosterage, captive disputation, and recognition form a compact answer panel with its own internal resolution.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Because the first image answers 49:14-21, the sibling relation must remain visible even with a separate chunk.

primary_reviews.support: The retrieval premortem sees unresolved continuity from Zion's complaint through the legal questions of 50:1-3.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Formula and question-answer evidence support the local unit, but only under compulsory 49:14-50:3 context.

challenge.claim: The children-and-captors panel may be misleading without the larger Zion-to-legal sequence.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Keep 49:22-26 searchable only with mandatory hydration through 49:14-50:3.

deciding_marker_or_seam: legal questions reach creation-darkness power answer
boundary_rationale: Accept 50:1-3 as a legal disputation ending in a creation-power answer. Family imagery links backward to Zion, but imagery alone cannot erase the chapter-opening questions or merge them into the disciple's first-person speech.
defensible_basis: The divine legal questions about a divorce document and creditors begin at 50:1, shift to the absence of an answer, and culminate in sea-drying and heavenly-darkness claims. Verse 4 then changes to a first-person taught-tongue testimony with a different form.

source_observations.text: Yahweh says, “Where is the bill of your mother’s divorce, with which I have put her away? Or to which of my creditors have I sold you? Behold, you were sold for your iniquities, and your mother was put away for your transgressions.
I clothe the heavens with blackness. I make sackcloth their covering.”

primary_reviews.support: Interrogatives about bill, creditor, calling, and shortened hand govern verses 1-2; first-person power claims in verses 2-3 answer them.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The abrupt transition at verse 4 is clear, while the backward addressee relation to Zion is less explicit.

primary_reviews.support: A legal accusation is followed by rhetorical proof of redeeming power, producing a complete question-and-answer disputation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The unit is very short and therefore depends on the 49:14-50:3 parent for its family-personification context.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical and retrieval review emphasizes the uninterrupted Zion-family problem across the chapter seam.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The new legal form remains defensible as a child if its upstream complaint and restoration answer travel with it.

challenge.claim: Separating 50:1-3 may conceal that the mother and children imagery continues from chapter 49.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Never surface 50:1-3 without the 49:14-50:3 operational parent.

deciding_marker_or_seam: taught-tongue testimony continues through two audience exhortations and fire warning
boundary_rationale: Accept 50:4-11 as one disciple-servant testimony with its audience exhortations. The verse-10 vocative is a strong internal seam, but cutting there would detach the two responses from the witness that defines whom they are asked to trust.
rejected_alternative: split at 50:10 without parent or decide speaker identity
defensible_basis: The taught-tongue testimony begins at verse 4 and proceeds through opened ear, suffering, help, and courtroom confidence; verses 10-11 then address two audiences as the testimony's practical alternatives. The self-lit-fire warning closes the governed speech.

source_observations.text: The Lord Yahweh has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary. He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.

Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who adorn yourselves with torches around yourselves, walk in the flame of your fire, and among the torches that you have kindled. You will have this from my hand: you will lie down in sorrow.

primary_reviews.support: Although the mi-bakhem question changes the addressee at verse 10, the two audience responses remain governed by the taught-tongue testimony and its trust contrast, supporting one hydrated 50:4-11 unit.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The warning at verse 11 still depends on the preceding servant voice and shares the unit's final evaluative function.

primary_reviews.support: The primary distinguishes testimony in 4-9 from audience alternatives in 10-11 because person, addressee, and function change.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A whole-unit presentation better protects the exhortations from becoming detached moral sayings.

challenge.claim: The direct question in 50:10 opens a new rhetorical form.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Permit two hydrated children if downstream retrieval can always supply both siblings.

primary_reviews.support: Later reuse of suffering and trust language cannot decide the testimony-exhortation seam or the speaker's identity.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Cross-reference pressure makes form-based hydration more important, not less.

deciding_marker_or_seam: repeated listen-hearken imperatives reach enduring-salvation close
boundary_rationale: Accept 51:1-8 as a three-summons comfort sequence. Atomizing each command would lose the cumulative movement from ancestral consolation through cosmic reversal to durable salvation, while verse 9 begins an unmistakable apostrophe to the divine arm.
defensible_basis: Three coordinated listening summonses address pursuers of righteousness, the people who know righteousness, and those fearing reproach; creation, instruction, and enduring salvation bind them. Verse 8 closes with moth-and-worm contrast before an awake appeal changes the voice.

source_observations.text: “Listen to me, you who follow after righteousness, you who seek Yahweh. Look to the rock you were cut from, and to the quarry you were dug from.
For the moth will eat them up like a garment, and the worm will eat them like wool; but my righteousness will be forever, and my salvation to all generations.”

primary_reviews.support: Repeated shim'u and haqshivu imperatives structure three linked panels, ending with the enduring-righteousness declaration in verse 8.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Different addressees and imperatives could justify internal indexing, but they remain coordinated within one reassurance sequence.

primary_reviews.support: The calls develop one argument: look to origins, attend coming instruction, and resist human reproach because salvation endures.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The sequence's internal triad should remain visible as stanza metadata rather than be erased by a single generic label.

primary_reviews.support: Abraham, creation, and salvation relations enrich the summonses without fixing separate retrieval units.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Familiar canonical themes could encourage extraction of one panel apart from its cumulative comfort logic.

deciding_marker_or_seam: awake-awake arm appeal reaches Zion-return refrain
boundary_rationale: Accept 51:9-11 as an apostrophe and return refrain. Merging it unmarked with 51:12-16 would confuse appeal with answer; splitting the exodus images from the return line would leave the petition without its envisioned result.
rejected_alternative: merge an unmarked voice with the divine answer
defensible_basis: The doubled 'awake' addresses the arm of YHWH, recalls sea-monster and exodus imagery, and resolves in the returning-ransomed refrain. Verse 12 answers with an emphatic divine 'I, I,' making the voice change an actual seam rather than a chapter convenience.

source_observations.text: Awake, awake, put on strength, arm of Yahweh! Awake, as in the days of old, the generations of ancient times. Isn’t it you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the monster?
Those ransomed by Yahweh will return, and come with singing to Zion. Everlasting joy shall be on their heads. They will obtain gladness and joy. Sorrow and sighing shall flee away.

primary_reviews.support: Uri-uri is a direct feminine imperative to the arm, whereas anokhi anokhi at 51:12 begins a first-person comfort response.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The return refrain also appears elsewhere in Isaiah and could be mistaken for a detachable liturgical fragment.

primary_reviews.support: A plea to awaken, remembered victory, and a confident return stanza form one short call whose answering voice follows immediately.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its dependence on 51:12-16 requires sibling hydration even though the boundary between voices is clear.

primary_reviews.support: The premortem specifically favored distinguishing the arm appeal from the divine answer while retaining their relation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Exodus and later reuse remain contextual parallels, not permission to isolate Rahab or the ransomed refrain.

deciding_marker_or_seam: I-I-am-your-comforter answer reaches you-are-my-people close
boundary_rationale: Accept 51:12-16 as the divine comfort answer. Its speaker formula and people declaration enclose the response; joining it to 51:9 would erase appeal-and-answer form, while extending to 51:17 would cross a fresh city vocative.
defensible_basis: The emphatic 'I, I am your comforter' answers the preceding appeal, challenges fear of mortals, recalls the maker, and ends by placing words in the addressee's mouth with 'you are my people.' The cup summons at verse 17 addresses Jerusalem anew.

source_observations.text: “I, even I, am he who comforts you. Who are you, that you are afraid of man who shall die, and of the son of man who will be made as grass?
I have put my words in your mouth and have covered you in the shadow of my hand, that I may plant the heavens, and lay the foundations of the earth, and tell Zion, ‘You are my people.’”

primary_reviews.support: Anokhi anokhi marks an emphatic answer, and the covenantal speech reaches a syntactic close in the words-in-mouth and people declaration.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Pronoun and addressee interpretation within verse 16 remains difficult even though the outer boundary is strong.

primary_reviews.support: The response moves from comfort through fear correction and creator memory to a renewed relation, answering rather than continuing the apostrophe.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its rhetoric depends on the preceding plea, so independent retrieval must include the awake-arm sibling.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical-premortem review endorsed the 51:9-11 appeal and 51:12-16 answer distinction under a shared parent.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Cross-references to creation or covenant cannot settle the difficult internal pronouns.

deciding_marker_or_seam: awake-stand-Jerusalem summons reaches cup transfer
boundary_rationale: Accept 51:17-23 as Jerusalem's cup-reversal speech. The repeated image binds accusation and rescue across all seven verses; extending across the chapter would combine two different awake addresses, while splitting at the rescue would sever reversal from crisis.
defensible_basis: The second awake command now addresses Jerusalem, develops the cup-of-wrath image through desolation and helpless sons, and reverses the cup onto tormentors. That transfer completes the city oracle before Zion receives a new awake command in 52:1.

source_observations.text: Awake, awake! Stand up, Jerusalem, you who have drunk from Yahweh’s hand the cup of his wrath. You have drunken the bowl of the cup of staggering, and drained it.

I will put it into the hand of those who afflict you, who have said to your soul, ‘Bow down, that we may walk over you;’ and you have laid your back as the ground, like a street to those who walk over.”

primary_reviews.support: Hit'oreri and qumi address Jerusalem directly, and the cup vocabulary continues until it is transferred in verse 23.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The following uri-uri to Zion repeats awakening language and creates a close sibling rather than unrelated material.

primary_reviews.support: City summons, devastation report, double calamity, announced advocacy, and cup transfer form a complete reversal oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The unit should retain its 51:17-52:6 paired-city parent because the next speech carries restoration forward.

primary_reviews.support: The premortem rejected the old 51:9-52:12 superchunk and recognized this cup-reversal movement separately.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Canonical cup imagery supplies comparison only and must not determine the seam.

deciding_marker_or_seam: second awake-awake summons reaches know-my-name close
boundary_rationale: Accept 52:1-6 as an awake-Zion redemption oracle. The name-recognition promise is its explanatory close; merging it into the herald poem would blur a direct imperative to the city with the narrator's celebration of good news on the mountains.
defensible_basis: A second doubled awake summons now names Zion and Jerusalem, commands release from dust and bonds, and explains the people's sale, oppression, and coming recognition of the divine name. Verse 7's herald scene replaces direct city address with an arriving messenger.

source_observations.text: Awake, awake! Put on your strength, Zion. Put on your beautiful garments, Jerusalem, the holy city, for from now on the uncircumcised and the unclean will no more come into you.
Therefore my people shall know my name. Therefore they shall know in that day that I am he who speaks. Behold, it is I.”

primary_reviews.support: Uri-uri followed by Zion and Jerusalem vocatives opens the speech, while 'my people shall know my name' finishes the divine explanation in verse 6.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The repeated awakening vocabulary deliberately relates this unit to 51:17-23 and should not be treated as a wholly new macro-cycle.

primary_reviews.support: Enthronement clothing, release commands, historical explanation, and promised name recognition produce a complete redemption address.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The prose-like explanation in verses 3-6 shifts texture but remains governed by the city's awakening summons.

primary_reviews.support: The premortem identified 52:1-6 between Jerusalem's cup reversal and the herald proclamation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later Zion and redemption parallels cannot replace the local vocatives as seam evidence.

deciding_marker_or_seam: how-beautiful herald scene reaches bared-arm universal sight
boundary_rationale: Accept 52:7-10 as a herald-and-enthronement poem. Its watchmen and universal audience belong together, whereas separating famous herald language through later citation would fracture the movement before the bared-arm conclusion.
rejected_alternative: let later citation dictate a seam
defensible_basis: The exclamation over beautiful feet introduces a mountain herald, watchmen answering together, Zion's comfort, and YHWH baring an arm before all nations. Universal sight in verse 10 finishes the proclamation; the doubled departure imperative at verse 11 starts a different action.

source_observations.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news, who proclaims salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
Yahweh has made his holy arm bare in the eyes of all the nations. All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.

primary_reviews.support: Mah-na'wu begins the herald exclamation, and the chain from good news to watchmen to revealed arm closes with all ends seeing in verse 10.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The departure imperatives at 52:11 remain tightly related as the response expected from the announced reign.

primary_reviews.support: The literary primary groups herald, enthronement, and departure as 52:7-12 because proclamation and response form one exodus movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The new imperative sequence at verse 11 is sufficiently distinct to justify children if both remain hydrated.

challenge.claim: Verses 7-12 may be one proclamation-and-departure unit.
