primary_reviews.counterevidence: Canonical quotation of the herald must not narrow the unit to a single verse.

deciding_marker_or_seam: depart-depart imperative reaches divine rear-guard close
boundary_rationale: Accept 52:11-12 as a departure coda under compulsory 51:1-52:12 hydration. The doubled imperative opens a new response to the herald, and the front-and-rear-guard statement closes it; a one-verse extraction would split command from assurance.
defensible_basis: The repeated 'depart' commands initiate a compact exodus summons: leave, touch no unclean thing, purify yourselves, and go without panic because YHWH leads and guards. Both verses are necessary; neither has a self-contained function when retrieved alone.

source_observations.text: Depart! Depart! Go out from there! Touch no unclean thing! Go out from among her! Cleanse yourselves, you who carry Yahweh’s vessels.
For you shall not go out in haste, neither shall you go by flight; for Yahweh will go before you, and the God of Israel will be your rear guard.

primary_reviews.support: Suru suru and tse'u are plural imperatives at 52:11, answered by front-guard and rear-guard participial claims in verse 12.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its brevity makes paragraph evidence insufficient for naked retrieval; parent and herald sibling are mandatory.

primary_reviews.support: The literary proposal retains 52:7-12 so the announcement and commanded departure remain one movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A discrete imperative form exists at verse 11, but it should not be presented without the herald.

challenge.claim: The two-verse summons may be an internal coda rather than an independent child.
challenge.proposed_remedy: If surfaced, always hydrate 52:11-12 with 52:7-10 and the 51:1-52:12 parent.

primary_reviews.support: The review recognized the departure summons as a distinct response but rejected naked verse retrieval.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Exodus parallels clarify function without granting either verse autonomous status.

deciding_marker_or_seam: behold-my-servant opening reaches final allotment close
boundary_rationale: Accept 52:13-53:12 as one servant poem at high boundary confidence while preserving textual uncertainty inside it. Chapter division and later quotation are both rejected as seam authorities; dividing the report from the concluding speech would dismantle the poem's answer structure.
rejected_alternative: split at chapter or later reuse
defensible_basis: 'Behold, my servant shall act wisely' opens a presentation that passes through astonished nations, communal report, suffering, death, outcome, and a concluding divine allotment. The English chapter break interrupts no voice or form, and the final bearing-of-sin statement supplies the poem's close.

source_observations.text: Behold, my servant will deal wisely. He will be exalted and lifted up, and will be very high.

Therefore I will give him a portion with the great. He will divide the plunder with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was counted with the transgressors; yet he bore the sins of many and made intercession for the transgressors.

primary_reviews.support: Hen yaskil 'avdi begins the presentation, first-person plural report dominates 53:1-6, and the final first-person allotment in 53:11-12 closes the frame.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: OSHB and UXLC share a Leningrad-family base; they cannot independently resolve 52:15, 53:8, 53:10, or the WEB footnote about 'light' in 53:11.

primary_reviews.support: Presentation, audience reaction, communal confession, narrated suffering and burial, then evaluative conclusion constitute an indivisible poetic sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Many famous lines have independent reception histories, creating exceptional extraction pressure despite the coherent form.

primary_reviews.support: Extensive canonical reuse confirms dense relations but cannot create seams or decide the servant's identity.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A later quotation may begin or end midmovement, so its bounds must not be projected onto Isaiah.

deciding_marker_or_seam: sing-barren address reaches covenant-of-peace close
boundary_rationale: Accept 54:1-10 as the barren-Zion restoration and covenant reassurance. Ending with the unshaken peace covenant respects the completed marriage-and-mercy argument; whole-chapter retrieval alone would hide the new visual and architectural form at verse 11.
defensible_basis: The barren woman's song-command opens a city restoration movement through enlarged tents, reversal of shame, renewed marriage imagery, flood comparison, and the covenant of peace. Verse 11 changes the addressee to an afflicted, storm-tossed city and begins the jeweled rebuilding panel.

source_observations.text: “Sing, barren, you who didn’t give birth! Break out into singing, and cry aloud, you who didn’t travail with child! For more are the children of the desolate than the children of the married wife,” says Yahweh.
For the mountains may depart, and the hills be removed, but my loving kindness will not depart from you, and my covenant of peace will not be removed,” says Yahweh who has mercy on you.

primary_reviews.support: Ranni 'aqarah is a feminine singular command, and the mercy-oath sequence reaches a covenantal close at 54:10.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: City and woman metaphors continue into verse 11, so the division reflects form change rather than a new referent ruling.

primary_reviews.support: Song, expansion, shame reversal, spouse reassurance, flood analogy, and peace covenant form a sustained restoration address.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A whole-chapter parent remains useful because both children portray the same afflicted-restored city.

primary_reviews.support: Covenant and flood relations illuminate the reassurance but do not determine the verse-10 endpoint.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later use of the barren-woman language could encourage extracting verse 1 from its complete restoration movement.

deciding_marker_or_seam: afflicted-one reset reaches servants' heritage close
boundary_rationale: Accept 54:11-17 as the jeweled-city and protected-servants panel. It has an independent address and concluding ownership formula; merging all chapter 54 would flatten the change from marital covenant reassurance to architecture, security, and communal heritage.
defensible_basis: The vocative 'afflicted, storm-tossed, and not comforted' resets the imagery to jeweled foundations, taught children, established righteousness, failed attackers, and the heritage of YHWH's servants. The final heritage declaration in verse 17 closes this city-protection oracle.

source_observations.text: “You afflicted, tossed with storms, and not comforted, behold, I will set your stones in beautiful colors, and lay your foundations with sapphires.

No weapon that is formed against you will prevail; and you will condemn every tongue that rises against you in judgment. This is the heritage of Yahweh’s servants, and their righteousness is of me,” says Yahweh.

primary_reviews.support: The feminine vocative at 54:11 starts a new description, and the concluding zot nachalat 'avde YHWH formula marks ownership and closure.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The same city addressee continues from 54:1-10, limiting how independently this child should be presented.

primary_reviews.support: Jeweled construction, taught descendants, righteousness, failed weapons, and servant heritage comprise a complete protected-city oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later interpretations of the stones or servants cannot decide the city's identity or subdivide the list.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical city and foundation imagery is relation evidence only; it neither names the community nor sets an internal seam.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The protected-servants close may be quoted separately, so hydration with the afflicted-city opening is important.

deciding_marker_or_seam: all-who-thirst invitation reaches nations-running close
boundary_rationale: Accept 55:1-5 as the water-food invitation and covenant appeal. The nations-running conclusion belongs with the David covenant statement it develops, while retaining all chapter 55 would conceal the new imperative, wicked-person address, and creation procession that follow.
defensible_basis: The cry to everyone who thirsts initiates an invitation to water, food, attentive hearing, life, covenant, and nations; the unknown nation's running response completes the appeal in verse 5. The seek command in verse 6 changes from invitation and covenant offer to urgent return.

source_observations.text: “Hey! Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
Behold, you shall call a nation that you don’t know; and a nation that didn’t know you shall run to you, because of Yahweh your God, and for the Holy One of Israel; for he has glorified you.”

primary_reviews.support: Hoy kol-tsame begins a public invitation, and the covenant-witness-nations syntax reaches its result in the running nation of verse 5.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The imperative series continues at verse 6, so the two halves remain closely coordinated within chapter 55.

primary_reviews.support: Invitation, rhetorical challenge, listening, covenant assurance, witness language, and international response form one offer sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Food and water images tempt devotional extraction, but their literary function depends on hearing and covenant.

primary_reviews.support: Davidic and nations relations are context for the invitation; they do not establish where the next exhortation begins.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later citation of the thirst invitation cannot reduce the unit to its opening verse.

deciding_marker_or_seam: seek-YHWH reset reaches everlasting-sign creation procession
boundary_rationale: Accept 55:6-13 as a seek-return and effective-word procession. Isolating the thoughts or word sayings would break their argumentative placement between repentance and transformed creation; verse 13's sign statement supplies the actual terminus.
defensible_basis: 'Seek YHWH while he may be found' begins an exhortation to return, explains divine compassion and the distance between thoughts, compares the effective word to rain, and ends with joyful departure and an everlasting sign. The sequence proceeds from human response to divine efficacy and creation's answer.

source_observations.text: Seek Yahweh while he may be found. Call on him while he is near.
Instead of the thorn the cypress tree will come up; and instead of the brier the myrtle tree will come up. It will make a name for Yahweh, for an everlasting sign that will not be cut off.”

primary_reviews.support: Dirshu and the return imperatives open the section, while the ki-asher comparison develops through word accomplishment to the everlasting-sign close.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Several proverb-like lines can appear self-contained in translation, but their Hebrew connectors maintain the argument.

primary_reviews.support: Exhortation, mercy rationale, thought comparison, rain-word analogy, and celebratory exodus make a carefully linked movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The shift from direct address to extended simile is internal development, not evidence for famous-saying chunks.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical uses of divine word or exodus imagery cannot select an internal boundary in this argument.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Retrieval must keep the effective-word analogy attached to both return and its creation-level outcome.

deciding_marker_or_seam: thus-says justice exhortation reaches gather-others close
boundary_rationale: Accept 56:1-8 as a justice-Sabbath and outsider-gathering oracle. The unit's boundary follows addressee and form, not a policy conclusion; extending into verse 9 would cross from promised inclusion to animal summons and leadership satire.
rejected_alternative: infer policy or theology from retrieval boundary
defensible_basis: A messenger formula introduces commands to keep justice and righteousness, a Sabbath beatitude, speeches to foreigner and eunuch, a promised memorial, and an ingathering declaration. 'I will gather others to him' in verse 8 completes the widening movement before beasts are summoned against failed watchmen.

source_observations.text: Yahweh says: “Maintain justice and do what is right, for my salvation is near and my righteousness will soon be revealed.
The Lord Yahweh, who gathers the outcasts of Israel, says, “I will yet gather others to him, in addition to his own who are gathered.”

primary_reviews.support: Koh amar YHWH begins the exhortation, and the participial gatherer formula in verse 8 closes the foreigner-eunuch-gathering sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Terms for Sabbath, foreigner, eunuch, and memorial carry translation and social-context questions that do not invalidate the outer seam.

primary_reviews.support: Justice command, blessing, two anticipated objections, direct reassurance, house-of-prayer promise, and final gathering claim form a complete inclusion oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The list could be overatomized by addressee; the repeated gathering purpose keeps it whole.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical and policy questions lie outside the chunking authority and cannot determine this boundary.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The retrieval rationale must avoid turning the selected unit into a normative ruling about later communities.

deciding_marker_or_seam: beast summons and failed-watchmen satire reach righteous-rest notice across chapter
boundary_rationale: Hold 56:9-57:2 as the surfaced unit rather than force a verse-boundary answer. Splitting at the chapter would separate the righteous-death notice from the failed-leader context it may close, yet folding it permanently backward would conceal a plausible transition toward 57:3.
defensible_basis: The beast summons at 56:9 opens a satire on blind watchmen, mute dogs, greedy shepherds, and their drinking boast; 57:1-2 then notices the righteous person's death and rest. Because that notice can either condemn public indifference or begin a new contrast, the cross-chapter parent remains held.

source_observations.text: All you animals of the field, come to devour, all you animals in the forest.
He enters into peace. They rest in their beds, each one who walks in his uprightness.

hold.question: Does the righteous-death notice close or contrast the failed-watchmen indictment, or begin the following community accusation?
options: retain 56:9-57:2 as the only surfaced unit
hold.requested_reviewer: independent Hebrew discourse and prophetic-satire specialist plus human/external-AI adjudicator

primary_reviews.support: The beast vocative and participial watchmen satire are clear, but ha-tsaddiq 'avad at 57:1 changes subject abruptly and can initiate a new observation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Correlated OSHB and UXLC views cannot provide independent witness convergence for the discourse attachment.

challenge.claim: The function of 57:1-2 relative to the watchmen satire remains unsettled.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Compare 56:9-12 plus 57:1-2 children against the held parent using independent Hebrew discourse evidence.

primary_reviews.support: Leadership satire followed by ignored righteous death makes a coherent indictment-and-consequence reading at the larger level.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A separately retrievable death-and-rest notice is also a defensible form if the failed-watchmen parent always accompanies it.

primary_reviews.support: Premortem review identified this exact cross-chapter attachment as a hot zone and rejected silent chapter fallback.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Relations to other shepherd or righteous-death passages cannot decide whether the notice closes or opens.

deciding_marker_or_seam: fresh direct offspring vocative reaches wind-and-refuge close
boundary_rationale: Accept 57:3-13 as an idolatrous-offspring accusation. Its direct vocative distinguishes it from the death notice, and the wind-versus-refuge verdict finishes the case; keeping only a 56:9-57:13 superchunk would bury this sharp addressee reset.
defensible_basis: The command 'draw near here' addresses a new accusatory audience and develops mockery, cultic sites, bed imagery, diplomatic journeys, exposure, and a final contrast between wind-carried works and refuge. The refuge-inheritance sentence at verse 13 closes the prosecution.

source_observations.text: “But draw near here, you sons of a sorceress, you offspring of adulterers and prostitutes.

When you cry, let those whom you have gathered deliver you, but the wind will take them. A breath will carry them all away, but he who takes refuge in me will possess the land, and will inherit my holy mountain.”

primary_reviews.support: We'atem qirvu-hennah opens a direct plural accusation, and the wind/refuge antithesis completes it in 57:13.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Rare cultic and sexual euphemisms introduce translation uncertainty inside the speech without weakening its outer address.

primary_reviews.support: Vocative, taunting questions, location catalogue, political-cultic exposure, and refuge contrast constitute a full accusation oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Individual images must not become tiny chunks because their force accumulates toward the closing verdict.

primary_reviews.support: The premortem required separation from 56:9-57:2 while preserving the 56:9-57:13 context relation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Other idolatry passages may clarify imagery but cannot set this seam or identify historical groups.

deciding_marker_or_seam: build-up imperative reaches contrite healing and no-peace coda
boundary_rationale: Accept 57:14-21 as a road-building and contrite-healing oracle ending in contrast. Dividing healing from the wicked-sea conclusion would remove the negative foil that completes the promise; extending backward would cross the refuge verdict and a new proclamation form.
defensible_basis: The road-building imperative initiates a proclamation about the high and holy one dwelling with the contrite, limits divine contention, recounts wrath and healing, and contrasts peace with the tossing wicked sea. The no-peace statement at verse 21 provides a deliberate refrain-like close.

source_observations.text: He will say, “Build up, build up, prepare the way! Remove the stumbling-block out of the way of my people.”
“There is no peace”, says my God, “for the wicked.”

primary_reviews.support: Solu solu and pannu-derekh open with plural imperatives, while 'no peace' seals the righteous/wicked contrast in verse 21.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: First-person shifts between wrath, hiding, seeing, and healing make internal movements but not separate speeches.

primary_reviews.support: Preparation command, transcendence-and-contrition claim, limited wrath, healing, created praise, and sea contrast form one balanced oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The positive healing panel could be excerpted, but the final contrast supplies its literary completion.

primary_reviews.support: Peace and contrition relations do not establish an internal boundary or decide the subjects addressed.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The no-peace refrain also connects to 48:22, a relation that should not merge noncontiguous units.

deciding_marker_or_seam: cry-aloud commission reaches restored-foundations close
boundary_rationale: Accept 58:1-12 as the false-fast and justice disputation with its promised outcomes. Ending before verse 13 preserves the difference between the communal fast critique and the separate foot-and-Sabbath condition; whole-chapter retrieval would hide that functional reset.
defensible_basis: The cry-aloud commission opens a dispute over apparent devotion and fasting, contrasts exploitation with release and care, then develops conditional light, guidance, rebuilding, and restored-path names. Verse 12 completes the justice-to-restoration argument before a new Sabbath condition begins.

source_observations.text: “Cry aloud! Don’t spare! Lift up your voice like a trumpet! Declare to my people their disobedience, and to the house of Jacob their sins.
Those who will be of you will build the old waste places. You will raise up the foundations of many generations. You will be called Repairer of the Breach, Restorer of Paths with Dwellings.

primary_reviews.support: Qera be-garon begins the prophetic commission, repeated interrogatives structure the fast dispute, and rebuilding titles finish the conditional result in verse 12.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The if-then syntax continues in 58:13, so the chapter remains a strong operational parent.

primary_reviews.support: Complaint, counter-question, social indictment, chosen-fast definition, and restoration consequences form a complete disputation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The long result catalogue could be mistaken for several oracles, but it remains dependent on the preceding conditions.

primary_reviews.support: Review explicitly favored 58:1-12 and a separate Sabbath coda rather than one chapter fallback.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Ethical parallels elsewhere cannot authorize the seam or turn chunking into a policy judgment.

deciding_marker_or_seam: if-you-turn-your-foot condition reaches mouth-of-YHWH close
boundary_rationale: Accept 58:13-14 as a Sabbath conditional coda with mandatory 58:1-14 context. Its new condition and formal divine close justify retrieval, while isolation would detach the promise from the chapter's preceding critique of performative devotion.
defensible_basis: The conditional 'if you turn your foot from the Sabbath' introduces a compact coda about speech, delight, riding high, and feeding on Jacob's heritage. The mouth-of-YHWH formula closes it, but the two verses require chapter-parent hydration and should never appear as a naked saying.

source_observations.text: “If you turn away your foot from the Sabbath, from doing your pleasure on my holy day, and call the Sabbath a delight, and the holy of Yahweh honorable, and honor it, not doing your own ways, nor finding your own pleasure, nor speaking your own words,
then you will delight yourself in Yahweh, and I will make you to ride on the high places of the earth, and I will feed you with the heritage of Jacob your father;” for Yahweh’s mouth has spoken it.

primary_reviews.support: Im-tashiv introduces a new conditional protasis, and ki pi YHWH dibber supplies an explicit speech close.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Two-verse brevity and shared conditional rhetoric with verses 1-12 argue against unhydrated presentation.

primary_reviews.support: Foot, speech, delight, elevation, and inheritance constitute a concise conditional coda distinct from the fast disputation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its independence is functional rather than thematic; without the chapter parent it can be misconstrued as an isolated rule.

primary_reviews.support: Premortem review accepted the seam but questioned whether the coda should ever surface independently.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The explicit closing formula supports a child, provided retrieval always includes the fast-and-justice sibling.

challenge.claim: The Sabbath coda may be internal-only despite its formal closure.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Enforce 58:1-14 hydration and prohibit naked 58:13-14 retrieval.

deciding_marker_or_seam: hand-not-short opening reaches crooked-path conclusion
boundary_rationale: Accept 59:1-8 as ability defense and wrongdoing indictment. The person shift at verse 9 is a genuine seam; merging the confession would collapse accusation and self-inclusion, while stopping earlier would fragment a single governed catalogue.
defensible_basis: The declaration that YHWH's hand is not shortened answers an implied objection, then attributes separation to wrongdoing and expands into hands, lips, courts, eggs, webs, violent feet, and crooked paths. The no-peace conclusion at verse 8 ends the second-person indictment before 'therefore justice is far from us' changes to communal confession.

source_observations.text: Behold, Yahweh’s hand is not shortened, that it can’t save; nor his ear dull, that it can’t hear.
They don’t know the way of peace; and there is no justice in their ways. They have made crooked paths for themselves; whoever goes in them doesn’t know peace.

primary_reviews.support: Hen lo-qatsrah opens the ability defense, second- and third-person accusations dominate, and the crooked-path/no-peace close precedes a first-person plural turn.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Catalogue density produces many internal poetic lines, but none resets the governing indictment.

primary_reviews.support: Objection, causal answer, body-part catalogue, failed justice, hatching-weaving images, and violent path conclusion form one accusation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The vivid metaphors should remain internal features rather than become individually retrievable sayings.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical sin and path parallels do not decide where accusation becomes confession in Isaiah 59.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The first-person plural shift is stronger local evidence than any later quotation.

deciding_marker_or_seam: we-confession pivots inside 59:15 to divine observation intervention and covenant
boundary_rationale: Hold 59:9-21 as the active confession-to-intervention parent. A 9-15 and 16-21 split would assign the latter half of verse 15 to the wrong movement, yet ignoring the turn would erase two real forms; independent clause-sensitive review must choose the presentation.
rejected_alternative: force a false whole-verse seam at 15 and 16
defensible_basis: The communal 'therefore justice is far from us' begins confession and lament, but verse 15 turns inside the verse from missing truth to YHWH seeing and being displeased; intervention, armor, repayment, a redeemer, and covenant then follow. Verse granularity cannot represent the 15a/15b pivot honestly.

source_observations.text: Therefore justice is far from us, and righteousness doesn’t overtake us. We look for light, but see darkness; for brightness, but we walk in obscurity.

“As for me, this is my covenant with them,” says Yahweh. “My Spirit who is on you, and my words which I have put in your mouth shall not depart out of your mouth, nor out of the mouth of your offspring, nor out of the mouth of your offspring’s offspring,” says Yahweh, “from now on and forever.”

hold.question: Can a verse-only map split after verse 15 when the observer and intervention pivot begins at 15b, or must confession and intervention remain one surfaced unit?
options: surface 59:9-15 and 59:16-21 with explicit midverse approximation disclosure
retain 59:9-21 as the only surfaced unit
hold.requested_reviewer: independent Hebrew discourse/textual specialist and literary-form reviewer plus human/external-AI adjudicator

primary_reviews.support: At 59:15 the waw clause 'YHWH saw' begins divine observation after the communal account of absent truth; the pivot is intra-verse.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: OSHB and UXLC expose the same Leningrad-family wording, so they do not constitute independent textual confirmation.

challenge.claim: A verse-only route cannot place the confession/intervention seam exactly.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Compare whole 59:9-21 against disclosed approximate children 59:9-15 and 59:16-21 with external Hebrew review.

primary_reviews.support: Confession and divine-warrior intervention are distinct literary movements, and the latter begins before verse 16.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Keeping the larger unit avoids a false exact seam but reduces direct retrieval of the two forms.

challenge.claim: The active parent suppresses a genuine midverse form change.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Retain the hold until clause-level boundaries or an explicit approximation policy is authorized.

primary_reviews.support: The premortem preferred whole 59:1-21 at verse granularity or a disclosed hold rather than a confident split.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Redeemer and covenant relations later in canon cannot repair the local midverse problem.

challenge.claim: Canonical reuse may bias reviewers toward starting the intervention too late.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Adjudicate only from Isaiah's discourse and direct textual evidence, with 59:15b named explicitly.

deciding_marker_or_seam: arise-shine summons reaches the ships procession
boundary_rationale: Accept 60:1-9 as the illumination and gathering procession. A whole-chapter chunk would hide the transition from arriving peoples and ships to reconstruction, gate policy, and renamed civic space, while extracting light verses would sever them from the returning children.
defensible_basis: The arise-and-shine command opens Zion's illumination, nations and kings approaching, children returning, abundance arriving, and ships bringing sons from afar. Verse 9 completes the first maritime procession; foreign builders and open gates begin a new city-administration panel at verse 10.

source_observations.text: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory has risen on you!

Surely the islands will wait for me, and the ships of Tarshish first, to bring your sons from far away, their silver and their gold with them, for the name of Yahweh your God, and for the Holy One of Israel, because he has glorified you.

primary_reviews.support: Qumi ori is a feminine city summons; deictic gathering and sea-wealth language proceed through the ships and sons in verse 9.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 10 continues nations-and-kings material, so the seam depends on movement and function rather than a wholly new addressee.

primary_reviews.support: Light, nations, children, abundance, animal procession, and ships form an arrival sequence that reaches a visible pause.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The catalogue can feel expansive enough to absorb the chapter, but later verses shift from procession to rebuilt city order.

primary_reviews.support: Later light and nations imagery supplies relations but no independent verse-9 boundary.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Famous arise-shine retrieval is a major premortem risk unless the gathering procession travels with it.

deciding_marker_or_seam: builders-and-kings reset reaches renamed walls and gates
boundary_rationale: Accept 60:10-18 as the rebuilding-and-transformed-city movement. Verse 19 starts a different everlasting-light coda with the sun and moon; merging it here would blur civic reconstruction and renaming with a new cosmic illumination claim.
defensible_basis: Foreigners building walls and kings serving the city open a new administrative panel: gates remain open, hostile nations face judgment, wealth enters, former oppressors bow, and violence gives way to renamed walls and gates. The paired names Salvation and Praise finish the transformation at verse 18.

source_observations.text: “Foreigners will build up your walls, and their kings will serve you; for in my wrath I struck you, but in my favor I have had mercy on you.
Violence shall no more be heard in your land, nor desolation or destruction within your borders; but you will call your walls Salvation, and your gates Praise.

primary_reviews.support: The subject shift to foreign builders at 60:10 begins the panel, and the naming clause for walls and gates gives verse 18 a formal civic close.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Nations and kings continue from verses 1-9, so the unit remains a functional child of the full Zion procession.

primary_reviews.support: Construction, open gates, tribute, reversed domination, material transformation, and renamed defenses form a complete city-order sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The many catalogue items should not be separated merely because each has vivid imagery.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical city and gate parallels offer hydration but cannot establish the verse-18 ending.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later ideal-city imagery could cause thematic mega-clustering across the clear light reset at verse 19.

deciding_marker_or_seam: no-more-sun-moon reset reaches little-one mighty-nation close
boundary_rationale: Accept 60:19-22 as the everlasting-light coda. Its cosmic-light opening is not another item in the building catalogue, and extracting only verse 19 would lose the mourning, people, land, and divine-timing conclusions that complete the stanza.
defensible_basis: The declaration that sun and moon will no longer provide the city's light begins a compact finale about everlasting illumination, ended mourning, universal righteousness, enduring possession, and accelerated growth. 'I, YHWH, will hasten it' closes the chapter and the panel.

source_observations.text: The sun will be no more your light by day, nor will the brightness of the moon give light to you, but Yahweh will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your glory.
The little one will become a thousand, and the small one a strong nation. I, Yahweh, will do this quickly in its time.”

primary_reviews.support: Lo-yihyeh-lakh 'od begins a negative future contrast with prior city conditions, and the first-person hastening statement closes verse 22.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Light imagery links backward to 60:1, making the whole chapter a strong ring-shaped parent.

primary_reviews.support: Cosmic illumination, transformed mourning, righteous inhabitants, planted possession, and accelerated population create a short chapter finale.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Because every line is memorable, the risk is verse-level extraction rather than undersegmentation.

primary_reviews.support: Later canonical light imagery cannot decide whether Isaiah's coda starts at verse 19 or identify its subjects.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The local no-longer contrast and chapter-closing divine signature remain the proper evidence.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Spirit-upon-me self-report reaches planting-and-glory purpose
boundary_rationale: Accept 61:1-3 as a proclamation commission without identifying the speaker. Verse 4 changes from first-person task report to third-person rebuilding outcomes; later quotation may illuminate reception but cannot shorten or redefine Isaiah's complete commission.
rejected_alternative: use later citation to identify speaker
defensible_basis: The first-person report 'the Spirit of the Lord YHWH is on me' introduces an anointing and a chain of proclamation assignments to the poor, brokenhearted, captives, mourners, and Zion. The naming of oaks of righteousness and the purpose of divine glory complete the commission in verse 3.

source_observations.text: The Lord Yahweh’s Spirit is on me, because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and release to those who are bound,

to provide for those who mourn in Zion, to give to them a garland for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness, that they may be called trees of righteousness, the planting of Yahweh, that he may be glorified.

primary_reviews.support: Ruah Adonai YHWH 'alay opens the self-report, and the infinitive chain ends in naming and planting purpose at 61:3.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: WEB notes an addition associated with LXX and DSS, but no pinned local primary LXX or DSS text is available to adjudicate wording.

primary_reviews.support: Anointing, commissioned announcements, reversals for mourners, new names, and a final glory purpose form one recognizable vocation speech.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The identity of the first-person voice is disputed and must remain separate from the form decision.

primary_reviews.support: Later citation of part of the commission neither supplies a local Isaiah seam nor settles the speaker.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Quotation bounds create a strong premortem hazard if projected backward onto verses 1-3.

deciding_marker_or_seam: they-shall-rebuild shift reaches recognized-offspring close
boundary_rationale: Accept 61:4-9 as a rebuilding, reversal, and covenant panel. Whole-chapter treatment would hide the shift to first-person rejoicing at verse 10, while splitting the social catalogue would detach its items from the covenant and recognized-seed resolution.
defensible_basis: 'They shall rebuild the old ruins' changes from commission to communal outcomes: reconstruction, changed labor relations, priestly naming, double inheritance, justice, covenant, and recognized offspring. The public recognition statement in verse 9 closes that promise sequence.

source_observations.text: They will rebuild the old ruins. They will raise up the former devastated places. They will repair the ruined cities that have been devastated for many generations.
Their offspring will be known among the nations, and their offspring among the peoples. All who see them will acknowledge them, that they are the offspring which Yahweh has blessed.”

primary_reviews.support: The third-person we-banu opening begins new activity, and the recognized-offspring clause in verse 9 completes the public-outcome panel.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Speaker and pronoun changes inside verses 7-8 are difficult but do not displace the outer shift at verses 4 and 10.

primary_reviews.support: Ruins, labor, role reversal, inheritance, justice, covenant, and offspring recognition form one restoration-result sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Individual social reversals may receive separate canonical attention, yet their function here is cumulative.

primary_reviews.support: Priestly, covenantal, and inheritance parallels cannot assign a boundary or identify a later community.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Retrieval should preserve the entire reversal catalogue rather than select one institutionally charged line.

deciding_marker_or_seam: I-greatly-rejoice reset reaches righteousness-praise garden simile
boundary_rationale: Accept 61:10-11 as a garment-and-garden praise coda. The emphatic rejoicing voice distinguishes it from the preceding plural promises; merging all chapter 61 would conceal that lyrical response, while naked retrieval would invite an unwarranted speaker ruling.
defensible_basis: 'I will greatly rejoice in YHWH' introduces a new first-person praise, using garments, bridegroom, bride, earth, and garden to celebrate righteousness and praise springing before nations. The two-verse hymn is complete but requires chapter and sibling hydration because its speaker is not identified.

source_observations.text: I will greatly rejoice in Yahweh! My soul will be joyful in my God, for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation. He has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself with a garland and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.
For as the earth produces its bud, and as the garden causes the things that are sown in it to spring up, so the Lord Yahweh will cause righteousness and praise to spring up before all the nations.

primary_reviews.support: Sos asis begins emphatic first-person rejoicing, and the earth-garden comparison carries the praise to the chapter close.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The shift does not identify whether the voice is individual, Zion, or communal; form alone cannot answer that question.

primary_reviews.support: Clothing and wedding similes lead into a germination image, creating a concise responsive hymn after the restoration promises.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Two-verse scale makes compulsory connection to 61:1-9 essential for responsible retrieval.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical garment, bride, and garden relations do not name the speaker or create smaller seams.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The coda's independence is literary, not permission to isolate an identity claim.

deciding_marker_or_seam: for-Zion-I-will-not-be-silent vow reaches bridegroom rejoicing
boundary_rationale: Accept 62:1-5 as Zion vindication, renaming, and marriage oracle. Verse 6 replaces the vow with installed watchmen and their charge; retaining the full chapter as one unit would hide this functional handoff.
defensible_basis: The vow not to be silent for Zion opens a movement toward visible righteousness, royal recognition, a new name, a crown, reversal of abandonment names, and marriage rejoicing. The bridegroom simile at verse 5 completes the renaming-and-delight argument before watchmen are introduced.

source_observations.text: For Zion’s sake I will not hold my peace, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest, until her righteousness shines out like the dawn, and her salvation like a burning lamp.
For as a young man marries a virgin, so your sons will marry you. As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you.

primary_reviews.support: Lema'an Tsiyyon lo eheseh initiates the vow, and the final bridegroom comparison resolves the Hephzibah-Beulah renaming in verse 5.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Zion remains the common subject through chapter 62, so the seam distinguishes rhetorical tasks rather than topics.

primary_reviews.support: Prophetic resolve, dawning vindication, public naming, crown imagery, reversed epithets, and marriage joy make a complete city oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The new-name sequence must stay together; atomizing individual names would destroy its reversal logic.

primary_reviews.support: Marriage and city-name relations elsewhere cannot decide Isaiah's internal unit or the vow's speaker.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later reception should not turn the boundary into an identification of Zion or the rejoicing figure.

deciding_marker_or_seam: walls-watchmen reset reaches court eating and drinking
boundary_rationale: Accept 62:6-9 as a watchmen charge joined to its sworn food-security answer. Verse 10 turns to gate-passing and highway commands; merging that procession would obscure the distinction between intercessory vigilance and public preparation.
defensible_basis: The declaration that watchmen have been set on Jerusalem's walls begins a charge to constant remembrance and prayer, followed by YHWH's oath that grain and wine will no longer feed enemies. Eating and drinking in the sacred courts complete the watchmen-and-harvest assurance.

source_observations.text: I have set watchmen on your walls, Jerusalem. They will never be silent day nor night. You who call on Yahweh, take no rest,
but those who have harvested it will eat it, and praise Yahweh. Those who have gathered it will drink it in the courts of my sanctuary.”

primary_reviews.support: The wall-watchmen clause introduces new agents, and the oath formula governs grain and wine until the court-consumption close.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Watchmen and oath panels could be indexed internally, but the promise is the answer to their unceasing charge.

primary_reviews.support: Appointment, no-silence command, pressure for Jerusalem's establishment, divine oath, and secured harvest form a compact assurance movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The repeated imperatives at verse 10 constitute a stronger new action than any internal division here.

primary_reviews.support: Watchman and oath parallels supply context but do not determine separate chunks in 62:6-9.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Retrieval must avoid treating the oath as an independent promise detached from the charged watchers.

deciding_marker_or_seam: pass-build-proclaim imperatives reach sought-not-forsaken names
boundary_rationale: Accept 62:10-12 as a highway-herald and naming finale. Its imperative barrage clearly begins after the harvest oath; splitting each name or proclamation would dismantle a single preparation-and-arrival sequence.
defensible_basis: The repeated commands to pass through gates, prepare a people's way, build a highway, remove stones, raise a banner, and proclaim to the earth launch the final procession panel. The four closing city-and-people names finish both the command and chapter.

source_observations.text: Go through, go through the gates! Prepare the way of the people! Build up, build up the highway! Gather out the stones! Lift up a banner for the peoples.
They will call them “The Holy People, Yahweh’s Redeemed”. You will be called “Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken”.

primary_reviews.support: Ivru ivru and sollu sollu create a new plural command cluster, while the final naming predicates provide closure.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Short commands and titles are internally segmented but function together as one procession preparation.

primary_reviews.support: Gate passage, road work, banner, global announcement, arriving reward, and new designations complete the chapter's public movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The names have lexical interest but no independent scene, speaker, or action warranting separate retrieval.

primary_reviews.support: Highway and herald relations elsewhere do not decide this local span or authorize name-by-name extraction.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The chapter's three children need a common 62:1-12 parent to preserve their progression.

deciding_marker_or_seam: who-is-this scene reaches winepress and recompense close
boundary_rationale: Accept 63:1-6 as the Edom-warrior dialogue without deciding the figure's identity or endorsing an ethical judgment. The Q-and-A frame and winepress monologue are inseparable; extending into verse 7 would cross from violent self-report to remembered mercies.
rejected_alternative: decide warrior identity or ethical judgment
defensible_basis: 'Who is this coming from Edom?' creates a question-and-answer scene about location, garments, strength, winepress, solitude, anger, and recompense. The warrior's final statement about pouring lifeblood on the earth ends the dialogue before a new communal remembrance begins at verse 7.

source_observations.text: Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? Who is this who is glorious in his clothing, marching in the greatness of his strength? “It is I who speak in righteousness, mighty to save.”
I trod down the peoples in my anger and made them drunk in my wrath. I poured their lifeblood out on the earth.”

primary_reviews.support: Mi-zeh opens an interrogative encounter, alternating questions and first-person answers until the completed recompense account in verse 6.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Rare color, blood, and winepress vocabulary creates translation pressure but no stronger internal seam.

primary_reviews.support: Arrival question, clothing question, solitary winepress explanation, appointed time, absent helper, and result constitute one dramatic dialogue.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The violence imagery must not be used to identify the speaker or convert the boundary into moral adjudication.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical warrior and winepress relations cannot identify this figure or alter Isaiah's dialogue frame.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later imagery may intensify extraction pressure around individual lines, so the complete exchange must remain intact.

deciding_marker_or_seam: I-will-mention opening reaches glorious-name close
boundary_rationale: Accept 63:7-14 as remembered-mercies and exodus praise. The 'look down from heaven' appeal at verse 15 creates the next mode; merging it backward would confuse narrated memory with present prayer, while ending early would truncate the guided-rest conclusion.
defensible_basis: 'I will mention the loving kindnesses of YHWH' changes voice and purpose from the warrior scene to remembered mercy, peoplehood, affliction, rebellion, remembered exodus, guidance, rest, and a glorious name. Verse 14 completes the historical praise before direct petition begins.

source_observations.text: I will tell of the loving kindnesses of Yahweh and the praises of Yahweh, according to all that Yahweh has given to us, and the great goodness toward the house of Israel, which he has given to them according to his mercies, and according to the multitude of his loving kindnesses.
As the livestock that go down into the valley, Yahweh’s Spirit caused them to rest. So you led your people to make yourself a glorious name.

primary_reviews.support: Hasde YHWH azkirah starts first-person praise, and the historical we/they sequence reaches the glorious-name purpose in verse 14.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Isaiah 63:9 contains textual and translation pressure that correlated local Hebrew views cannot independently settle.

primary_reviews.support: Mercy recital, filial expectation, affliction, rebellion, remembered deliverance, guided descent, and rest make a compact historical hymn.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The exodus recollection supplies the basis for the following plea, requiring a strong sibling relation.

primary_reviews.support: Exodus and wilderness parallels illuminate the recital but do not set a seam or harmonize wording.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The remembered history should not be divided according to later quotations of its components.

deciding_marker_or_seam: look-down-from-heaven pivot reaches final unanswered questions across versification
boundary_rationale: Accept 63:15-64:12 as one communal lament-prayer at high unit confidence, while lowering textual certainty inside it. A chapter split would sever the theophany plea from its kinship appeal; smaller famous-line units would fragment confession and the final appeal for response.
rejected_alternative: split at the chapter or WEB-MT seam
defensible_basis: The imperative to look down from heaven begins a communal lament that appeals to divine kinship, asks why wandering persists, pleads for a torn-heavens descent, confesses sin, invokes potter and people imagery, surveys ruined cities, and ends with unanswered questions. The prayer crosses the English chapter seam without changing voice.

source_observations.text: Look down from heaven, and see from the habitation of your holiness and of your glory. Where are your zeal and your mighty acts? The yearning of your heart and your compassion is restrained toward me.
Will you hold yourself back for these things, Yahweh? Will you keep silent and punish us very severely?

primary_reviews.support: Habbet mi-shamayim establishes the petition, and first-person plural address persists to the closing questions; however 63:19-64:1 versification and 63:9 textual pressure limit finer adjudication.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: OSHB and UXLC are correlated Leningrad-family representations, not independent witnesses for disputed wording or clause attachment.

primary_reviews.support: Heavenward appeal, father claim, wandering question, theophany request, remembered acts, confession, potter metaphor, devastation, and final interrogation form one prayer.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Internal turns are substantial, but none changes the praying community or resolves before the last question.

primary_reviews.support: Later use of the theophany and waiting language cannot dictate a chapter seam or a preferred textual reading.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The unit should expose its WEB-MT versification caution whenever retrieved.

deciding_marker_or_seam: sought-and-found opening reaches measured recompense close
boundary_rationale: Accept 65:1-7 as the answer-and-provocation catalogue. The measured-recompense sentence finishes the accusation; retaining 65:1-16 would hide the new-wine analogy and servants-versus-you structure that deliberately qualifies judgment.
defensible_basis: The divine answer opens with being sought and found by those not calling, then catalogs a continually provoking people through gardens, tombs, prohibited foods, separation claims, smoke imagery, and a measured promise to repay ancestral and present acts. Verse 8 starts a preservation analogy rather than continuing the indictment list.

source_observations.text: “I am inquired of by those who didn’t ask. I am found by those who didn’t seek me. I said, ‘See me, see me,’ to a nation that was not called by my name.

your own iniquities and the iniquities of your fathers together”, says Yahweh, “who have burned incense on the mountains, and blasphemed me on the hills. Therefore I will first measure their work into their bosom.”

primary_reviews.support: Nidrashti and nimtseti begin first-person response, and the measurement/recompense syntax closes the catalogue in verse 7.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The verbal voice and addressee of 65:1 are translation-sensitive, so the boundary cannot authorize an interpretation of who sought whom.

primary_reviews.support: Answer, outstretched-hands image, cultic-location catalogue, quoted separation, smoke, written record, and repayment form a complete indictment.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 8's cluster image creates a conspicuous rhetorical reset toward preservation and contrast.

primary_reviews.support: Later citation of 65:1 bears on reception but cannot identify the audience or fix internal seams.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The provocative practices should remain a governed catalogue rather than separate issue-based chunks.

deciding_marker_or_seam: new-wine cluster analogy reaches forgotten-former-troubles close
boundary_rationale: Accept 65:8-16 as the preserved-cluster and servants contrast. The analogy and repeated servant-versus-you pairs belong together; mapping those groups onto later communities would exceed chunking authority, and merging 1-16 would suppress the preservation reset.
rejected_alternative: map contrasting groups onto later communities
defensible_basis: The new-wine-in-a-cluster analogy begins a preservation movement, promises descendants and chosen possession, and contrasts servants with those who forsake YHWH through food, drink, joy, song, naming, and oath reversals. Forgotten former troubles close the contrast at verse 16.

source_observations.text: Yahweh says, “As the new wine is found in the cluster, and one says, ‘Don’t destroy it, for a blessing is in it:’ so I will do for my servants’ sake, that I may not destroy them all.

so that he who blesses himself in the earth will bless himself in the God of truth; and he who swears in the earth will swear by the God of truth; because the former troubles are forgotten, and because they are hidden from my eyes.

primary_reviews.support: Ka'asher yimmatse ha-tirosh introduces the cluster analogy, while the oath and forgotten-troubles language completes the servant contrast.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Group labels and second-person references remain interpretation-sensitive even though the repeated syntax is clear.

primary_reviews.support: Preservation analogy, chosen inheritance, abandoned table, four paired reversals, new naming, and forgotten distress create a controlled antiphonal oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The servant contrasts invite atomization, but their rhetorical force depends on cumulative parallelism.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical servant or remnant relations cannot identify the groups or choose a doctrinal reading.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The active seam rests on the cluster reset and repeated contrast, not later community mapping.

deciding_marker_or_seam: behold-I-create formula reaches holy-mountain close
boundary_rationale: Accept 65:17-25 as a new-creation and transformed-life oracle. Later apocalyptic reuse does not create a seam within Isaiah; separating lifespan, labor, prayer, or animal images would dismantle the single created-world vision.
rejected_alternative: let later apocalyptic reuse create a seam
defensible_basis: 'Behold, I create new heavens and a new earth' launches a creation oracle about forgotten former things, Jerusalem's joy, transformed lifespan, secure labor, answered prayer, animal peace, and the holy-mountain close. The chapter's final clause completes the catalogue before a throne-temple disputation begins.

source_observations.text: “For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things will not be remembered, nor come into mind.
The wolf and the lamb will feed together. The lion will eat straw like the ox. Dust will be the serpent’s food. They will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain,” says Yahweh.

primary_reviews.support: Hineni bore opens the creation declaration, and the lo-yare'u formula on the holy mountain closes verse 25.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Lifespan language in verse 20 and several verbal forms require translation caution without weakening the full oracle frame.

primary_reviews.support: New creation, city joy, reversed mortality, secure building and planting, answered call, and animal peace form one visionary catalogue.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Each image has substantial reception history, creating a predictable risk of theme-based microchunks.

primary_reviews.support: Later new-creation texts are relation evidence only and cannot dictate Isaiah's internal bounds.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The unit must remain non-authorizing about eschatological sequence or fulfillment.

deciding_marker_or_seam: heaven-throne questions reach chosen-delusions verdict
boundary_rationale: Accept 66:1-4 as a throne-temple and worship disputation. The chosen-delusions verdict closes the call-and-response failure; extending to verse 6 would mix indirect contrast with a direct community address, while the boundary itself authorizes no anti-temple theology.
defensible_basis: A throne-and-footstool declaration opens questions about building and rest, contrasts divine making with regard for the humble word-trembler, then reverses sacrificial acts and ends with chosen delusions because no one answered. Verse 5 addresses word-tremblers directly and begins another voice.

source_observations.text: Yahweh says: “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build to me? Where will I rest?

I also will choose their delusions, and will bring their fears on them, because when I called, no one answered; when I spoke, they didn’t listen, but they did that which was evil in my eyes, and chose that in which I didn’t delight.”

primary_reviews.support: Koh amar YHWH frames throne and house questions, and the ya'an clause explains the verdict through nonresponse at verse 4.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Sacrificial comparisons in verse 3 are syntactically dense and ethically charged, but they remain inside the disputation.

primary_reviews.support: Cosmic throne claim, house challenge, humble-person contrast, ritual reversals, and failed-call judgment make a complete argument.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The form must not be reduced to a topical temple passage or divided by each ritual example.

primary_reviews.support: Temple relations elsewhere cannot convert this chunk boundary into a judgment on worship or sacred space.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The direct word-trembler address at verse 5 is stronger seam evidence than broad temple themes.

deciding_marker_or_seam: hear-the-word vocative reaches temple recompense voice
boundary_rationale: Accept 66:5-6 as a word-tremblers and temple-recompense unit under final-cycle hydration. Merging through verse 16 would swallow the birth-and-comfort form; retrieving either verse alone would separate the audience promise from its audible outcome.
defensible_basis: 'Hear the word of YHWH, you who tremble at his word' introduces a persecuted audience, quotes hostile brothers, promises their shame, and then locates a tumultuous recompense voice in city and temple. The two verses operate as an address-and-soundscape hinge before Zion's birth poem.

source_observations.text: Hear Yahweh’s word, you who tremble at his word: “Your brothers who hate you, who cast you out for my name’s sake, have said, ‘Let Yahweh be glorified, that we may see your joy;’ but it is those who shall be disappointed.
A voice of tumult from the city, a voice from the temple, a voice of Yahweh that repays his enemies what they deserve.

primary_reviews.support: Shim'u debar YHWH with an explicit word-trembler vocative opens verse 5, and the triple qol sequence resolves in recompense at verse 6.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The brief hinge shares temple vocabulary backward and enemy judgment forward, so parent context is indispensable.

primary_reviews.support: Audience address, quoted mockery, promised appearance, and escalating city-temple-divine voices constitute a compact transitional oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its two-verse scale should not conceal the genuine speaker and scene reset before verse 7.

primary_reviews.support: Word-trembler and temple parallels do not establish an independent retrieval level for these verses.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Any surface must include siblings on both sides to avoid turning the hinge into a free-standing promise.

deciding_marker_or_seam: before-labor paradox reaches servants-enemies contrast
boundary_rationale: Accept 66:7-14 as Zion birth and maternal consolation. Birth, nursing, river, carrying, and mother-comfort imagery develop one poem to the hand-and-indignation hinge; splitting comfort from birth would remove the answer from its governing paradox.
defensible_basis: The paradoxical birth before labor begins a Zion-mother poem that asks who has heard such a thing, answers with sudden national birth, invites rejoicing and nursing, promises peace and glory, and ends with comfort, flourishing, and a servants-enemies contrast. Fire arrives only at verse 15.

source_observations.text: “Before she travailed, she gave birth. Before her pain came, she delivered a son.
You will see it, and your heart shall rejoice, and your bones will flourish like the tender grass. Yahweh’s hand will be known among his servants; and he will have indignation against his enemies.

primary_reviews.support: Beterem tahil begins the birth paradox, and the servant/enemy antithesis at verse 14 closes before the ki-hinneh fire arrival.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Pronouns and the relation between city, land, and people remain interpretive questions rather than seam authorities.

primary_reviews.support: Sudden birth, astonished questions, communal rejoicing, maternal feeding, peace-river promise, carrying, comfort, and flourishing create one coherent poem.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The imagery changes several times, but every development elaborates Zion's maternal reversal.

primary_reviews.support: Birth and mother-Zion parallels cannot identify referents or subdivide the poem.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later reuse should not extract a single birth or comfort line from its complete movement.

deciding_marker_or_seam: fire arrival and condemned rites meet abrupt 66:18 before nations mission worship and corpse finale
boundary_rationale: Hold 66:15-24 as the book-final parent. Surfacing 15-17 and 18-24 would respect judgment and nations-finale forms, yet correlated Hebrew witnesses cannot settle verse 18's ellipsis; the larger unit prevents a falsely exact seam while preserving both options for external review.
rejected_alternative: surface 15-17 and 18-24 before direct textual-literary review
defensible_basis: The fire-and-chariot arrival at verse 15 begins judgment and condemned-rite material, but verse 18 is syntactically abrupt: works and thoughts look backward while the gathering of nations looks forward to mission, enduring seed, worship, and the corpse image. The exact 17/18 attachment remains unresolved.

source_observations.text: For, behold, Yahweh will come with fire, and his chariots will be like the whirlwind; to give his anger with fierceness, and his rebuke with flames of fire.
“They will go out, and look at the dead bodies of the men who have transgressed against me; for their worm will not die, nor will their fire be quenched, and they will be loathsome to all mankind.”

options: surface 66:15-17 and 66:18-24 with compulsory shared-parent hydration
retain 66:15-24 as the only surfaced unit

primary_reviews.counterevidence: OSHB and UXLC represent the same Leningrad-family textual stream and cannot independently settle the elliptical attachment.
